items.title: The Model Has Preferences, but the Harness Got Controls - Part 1
items.summary: The Model Has Preferences. The Harness Has Controls. This is another collaboration between Usman Chaudhary and myself ; this time we decided to explore the mystery of “is harness a security boundary?” Part 1 of 3 on securing agents. The theme here is: we think that despite alignment efforts, models will make mistakes. The fix is not a better prompt or more more more alignment work. The fix includes a hard boundary around the model, and that boundary is the harness, in some cases. TL;DR Agent = Model + Harness. The model reasons and expresses preferences. The harness executes, and it is the primary execution boundary between model intent and real-world action. The model cannot be the security boundary. It is non-deterministic, it treats untrusted text as instructions, and it cannot police itself. A second “guard” model is a useful filter, not a wall. The harness is the boundary , the way a firewall and OS sandbox are boundaries for an application. It sits between the model and the enterprise gateway, and today it is the least mature and least watched layer in the stack. Fixing it requires two things: controlling what the agent can do through the harness (sandbox [which nobody should trust as a sole security boundary!], narrow identity, egress allowlists) and securing the harness itself as production software (configs, dependencies, and SIEM telemetry). This would be annoying to hear for some. 1. The Incident: A Database Gone in Nine Seconds Nine seconds. That is how long it took an AI coding agent at PocketOS in late April 2026 to delete the company’s production database and take the attached backups offline right alongside it. What happened, per Railway’s technical write-up : The agent hit a credential mismatch and went looking for a fix. It found a cloud API token that let it do far more than fix anything. It deleted the production database volume and made the attached snapshots unavailable — leaving PocketOS with three-month-old backups and a 60-hour recovery. Its own summary afterward was painfully candid, for a 2026 AI: “I guessed instead of verifying, I ran a destructive action without being asked.” The tempting question is the wrong one. ❌ Why did the model make a bad decision? Models will make bad decisions. Humans do too, and we have spent decades building controls that assume exactly that. “AI as insider” thinking works well here. ✅ Why was a bad decision allowed to become an irreversible action? This to us shows lack of security engineering, not “OMG is AI evil or what?” lamentations. This post argues that the answer lives in the agent harness, not the model. 2. How Agents Work: Model + Harness The most useful mental model for securing AI agents is also the simplest: Agent = Model + Harness . The model reasons. It is probabilistic. It predicts tokens, plans steps, and expresses preferences. It can be persuaded, confused, and tricked. The harness executes. It is everything that turns reasoning into action: the agent loop, shell and tool executors, MCP servers, repo config files, approval prompts, the OS sandbox, and (crucially) the credentials the agent runs with. Claude Code, Cursor, Codex CLI, Gemini CLI, and GitHub Copilot’s agent mode are all harnesses. 👉 A model that declines an action is expressing a preference. A harness that will not execute it is enforcing a control. That sentence is the thesis of this post. None of this is new security philosophy. Least privilege, isolation, identity, and audit logging are decades old. What agents change is where those principles must be enforced and how fast . Figure 1. Agent = Model + Harness. The model proposes actions; the five harness zones around it permit, block, or constrain them. 3. Why the Model Cannot Be the Security Boundary Let’s be blunt about something the industry keeps dancing around: the model will never be a reliable security boundary, and it is pointless to treat it as one. Three reasons, none fixable with a better system prompt: It is non-deterministic. The same input can produce a different action tomorrow. A boundary that holds 97% of the time is not a boundary; it is a statistic [I think Claude said this, sounds like it :-)]. Security boundaries are supposed to be boring and repeatable, not fun and adventurous. It consumes untrusted text as instructions. Agents read attacker-controlled text all day in READMEs, issues, PR comments, web pages, and tool descriptions, and models fail to reliably separate retrieved data from instructions . The UK NCSC calls LLMs “inherently confusable” ; OpenAI and Google both say prompt injection is “unlikely to ever be fully ‘solved’” . Model refusals help [as long as they reject attackers, not defenders, duh!], but they do not hold: in the Nx supply-chain attack , guardrails rejected roughly a quarter of Claude invocations and the attack still succeeded. It cannot police itself (self-review). Asking the actor model whether its own next action is safe is asking the suspect to run the investigation. And you do not need a rogue-AI scenario to see the risk: well-intentioned agents have already wiped production databases at Replit during a declared code freeze and at PocketOS, simply because their judgment failed and their blast radius was too wide. Maybe in the future it will, but not it cannot. “What about a second model that checks the first?” Simple, beautiful, “secure” model, right? Independent guard and reviewer models (Google’s Model Armor and the reviewer models OpenAI and Anthropic now ship inside their harnesses, as do many other security vendors) are a real risk-reduction layer, and we recommend them. But a reviewer model is still a probabilistic filter, not a final authorization boundary. You have stacked a second set of preferences on top of the first set: Anthropic’s own reviewer publishes a 17% false-negative rate across 52 real overeager actions. A useful filter, but not a wall, and not “a security invariant” for sure. The Appsec vs. Firewall Analogy We have been here before with web applications. Application security (secure coding, input validation, code review) makes the app harder to exploit, but every serious app still ships bugs — so we put runtime boundaries (firewalls, WAFs, OS sandboxes, IAM) around the app to enforce rules it cannot violate even when it is buggy or actively exploited. Agents work the same way: Model alignment, safety training, and prompting ≈ agent “appsec”/modelsec (fewer bad decisions, never zero). The harness ≈ runtime enforcement (sandbox [usually porous], tool policy, and IAM that keep bad decisions from becoming irreversible actions). 👉 The harness is the security boundary for the model , exactly as the firewall and sandbox are boundaries for the app — not because the model is bad, but because software fails. 4. Defense in Depth: Model, Harness, and Gateway Saying “the harness is the primary execution boundary” does not mean “only the harness matters.” In practice, an enterprise running agents relies on three control layers with distinct jobs: 1. The model (alignment, safety training, refusals). Run by the model vendor to reduce the rate of bad decisions . Probabilistic. 2. The harness (OS sandbox, tool policy, scoped identity, secrets handling, egress allowlist, approval gates, hooks, telemetry). Shipped by the AI vendor and configured by the customer to constrain all execution — both local and remote . 3. The enterprise agentic gateway (policy, identity brokering, MCP proxying, DLP, and logging across external model, tool, and data traffic). Run by the enterprise security team to centralize policy and SOC visibility across agents . Figure 2. Three control layers — and why local actions bypass the gateway. The harness mediates every proposed action; the enterprise gateway only sees traffic that leaves the endpoint. The layers are not interchangeable: ❌ A gateway does not see local endpoint execution. If a harness runs as the developer with — dangerously-skip-permissions, the gateway never sees a local rm -rf or secret read on a laptop. ❌ A harness alone does not give the SOC a cross-team control plane. And the harness is the least mature of the three. The model gets the research attention. The gateway is where enterprise vendors (ours included) are converging. The harness sits in the middle: shipped by AI vendors, configured by developers, treated as a productivity plugin, and mostly invisible to security. BTW, one of us (Anton) will revisit defense in depth in the age of AI soon ( this is one for cloud ). 👉 If the harness is the execution boundary, it has to be built, configured, and watched like one. 5. Where the Harness Fails Today Once you look at the harness as a security boundary rather than a developer convenience, three specific gaps stand out in how harnesses are deployed today. 1. Approval fatigue and bypass modes ( — yolo) A coding agent makes hundreds of tool calls in a single session. Ask a human to approve each one at machine speed and they stop reading within the hour: Anthropic measured users approving 93% of permission prompts before it introduced auto mode. A control that everyone clicks through is not a control. When friction gets too high, developers turn it off, and most major coding-agent harnesses expose an explicit bypass mode for exactly that ( — dangerously-skip-permissions in Claude Code, — yolo in Gemini CLI and Codex). 2. Over-privileged credentials and shared identity Today, local harnesses typically inherit the developer’s ambient git keys, cloud tokens, and MCP connections into Slack, GitHub, and production consoles. Unless sessions carry a separate agent identity, the agent’s blast radius equals the human’s — and the SOC cannot easily tell human and agent apart . 3. The harness itself is an unmonitored software attack surface Harness CVEs and bypasses Cursor’s MCPoison bound trust to a server’s name rather than its contents ( Tenable ). A GitHub Copilot exploit used prompt injection to flip on its own auto-approve setting ( Embrace The Red ). Even actively maintained harnesses ship bugs fast: Anthropic’s claude-code repository lists more than 30 security advisories . Weaponized configs and flags Agent config files are executable. In June 2026, the Miasma worm planted malicious configs across 73 Microsoft repositories that ran on open. No CVE required. In the Nx attack , which leaked 2,000+ verified secrets, the malware invoked victims’ own AI CLIs with bypass flags to do its reconnaissance. SOC blindness Harness telemetry is opt-in and redacts prompts and tool arguments by default ( Elastic Security Labs ). Copilot’s audit log omits local prompts entirely ( GitHub ). Raw chain-of-thought is never released to customers ( Anthropic ). 👉 The first two gaps are failures to contain what the agent can do . The third is a failure to protect and monitor the harness itself . 6. How to Secure the Harness: Three Architectural Moves Closing those gaps means doing two jobs at once: Controlling what the agent can do ( security within the harness ): enforcing hard limits on execution and reach so a bad model decision cannot become a catastrophe. Protecting the boundary itself ( security for the harness ): governing the harness’s code, configs, dependencies, and telemetry. A firewall with a remote code execution bug is not a boundary; neither is a harness whose config file can be rewritten by a README. In practice, that comes down to three architectural moves: Move A: Take enforcement out of the model. Run commands inside an OS sandbox with deterministic tool policy — backed by an independent, reasoning-blind reviewer model for judgment calls (stripped of the actor’s chain-of-thought so the agent cannot talk its way past the check) — with structured steering on blocked actions and human prompts reserved for irreversible ones. Move B: Shrink what the agent can reach. Give the agent its own identity, short-lived scoped tokens, secrets kept outside the sandbox, and an egress allowlist — breaking Simon Willison’s “lethal trifecta” of private data, untrusted content, and an outbound channel. Move C: Govern and watch the harness itself. Put agent config files under branch protection, pin MCP dependencies, and stream action telemetry and hooks to the SIEM. Figure 3. Where harnesses fail — and the three moves that fix them. Moves A and B contain what the agent can do; Move C governs the harness itself. Each move gets its own deep dive in Part 2 (hopefully!) 7. What the Harness Cannot Solve (Ever?) A boundary is only trustworthy if you are honest about where it ends. Prompt injection at the model layer remains unsolved. That is not a gap in the harness story; it is the premise of it. Every harness control assumes injection can succeed and asks what happens next. Bugs inside the vendor’s harness are the vendor’s to fix. Pick vendors who publish advisories and ship fixes fast, and treat harness updates like browser updates. The endpoint remains the thinnest layer. AI detection and response on developer laptops, where most harnesses actually run, is immature. Cloud-hosted sessions sidestep part of this; local agents do not. In other words, if you endpoints are owned, you need better host security, not “unbeatable” AI security (translation: it will get beaten anyway) Conclusion & What’s Next Strip away the new vocabulary and harness security is least privilege, isolation, identity, and logging, applied to a process that reads untrusted text and acts at machine speed. AI changes the speed of the attack, not the fundamentals of defense. 👉 The model will keep having preferences. The harness is where the controls go, and today it is the least watched layer in the stack. Coming next (hopefully!): Part 2: Three moves to secure the harness. Moves A, B, and C in detail: OS sandboxing and reviewer models (with the error and prompt-reduction rates vendors have published); dedicated identity, scoped tokens, and egress allowlists that break the lethal trifecta; and agent config as code, pinned MCP dependencies, and action telemetry in the SIEM. Part 3: Nobody owns the whole problem. The shared-responsibility split between model providers and enterprises, which vendors ship which control today, the prerequisites that have to be true first, and five actions for this quarter. Got comments? What stands between a coding agent’s bad decision and your production environment today? If the honest answer is “the model’s judgment,” you have a preference in a place where you need a control. P.S. This blog is ended up being very overengineered, but you can forgive us for this perhaps :-) The Model Has Preferences, but the Harness Got Controls - Part 1 was originally published in Anton on Security on Medium, where people are continuing the conversation by highlighting and responding to this story.

This is another collaboration between Usman Chaudhary and myself ; this time we decided to explore the mystery of “is harness a security boundary?”

Part 1 of 3 on securing agents. The theme here is: we think that despite alignment efforts, models will make mistakes. The fix is not a better prompt or more more more alignment work. The fix includes a hard boundary around the model, and that boundary is the harness, in some cases.

TL;DR

  • The model cannot be the security boundary. It is non-deterministic, it treats untrusted text as instructions, and it cannot police itself. A second “guard” model is a useful filter, not a wall.
  • The harness is the boundary, the way a firewall and OS sandbox are boundaries for an application. It sits between the model and the enterprise gateway, and today it is the least mature and least watched layer in the stack.
  • Fixing it requires two things: controlling what the agent can do through the harness (sandbox [which nobody should trust as a sole security boundary!], narrow identity, egress allowlists) and securing the harness itself as production software (configs, dependencies, and SIEM telemetry). This would be annoying to hear for some.
1. The Incident: A Database Gone in Nine Seconds

Nine seconds. That is how long it took an AI coding agent at PocketOS in late April 2026 to delete the company’s production database and take the attached backups offline right alongside it.

What happened, per Railway’s technical write-up:

  • The agent hit a credential mismatch and went looking for a fix.
  • It found a cloud API token that let it do far more than fix anything.
  • It deleted the production database volume and made the attached snapshots unavailable — leaving PocketOS with three-month-old backups and a 60-hour recovery.

Its own summary afterward was painfully candid, for a 2026 AI:

“I guessed instead of verifying, I ran a destructive action without being asked.”

The tempting question is the wrong one.

  • ❌ Why did the model make a bad decision? Models will make bad decisions. Humans do too, and we have spent decades building controls that assume exactly that. “AI as insider” thinking works well here.
  • ✅ Why was a bad decision allowed to become an irreversible action? This to us shows lack of security engineering, not “OMG is AI evil or what?” lamentations.

This post argues that the answer lives in the agent harness, not the model.

2. How Agents Work: Model + Harness

The most useful mental model for securing AI agents is also the simplest: Agent = Model + Harness.

  • The model reasons. It is probabilistic. It predicts tokens, plans steps, and expresses preferences. It can be persuaded, confused, and tricked.
  • The harness executes. It is everything that turns reasoning into action: the agent loop, shell and tool executors, MCP servers, repo config files, approval prompts, the OS sandbox, and (crucially) the credentials the agent runs with. Claude Code, Cursor, Codex CLI, Gemini CLI, and GitHub Copilot’s agent mode are all harnesses.

👉 A model that declines an action is expressing a preference. A harness that will not execute it is enforcing a control. That sentence is the thesis of this post.

None of this is new security philosophy. Least privilege, isolation, identity, and audit logging are decades old. What agents change is where those principles must be enforced and how fast.

Figure 1. Agent = Model + Harness. The model proposes actions; the five harness zones around it permit, block, or constrain them.3. Why the Model Cannot Be the Security Boundary

Let’s be blunt about something the industry keeps dancing around: the model will never be a reliable security boundary, and it is pointless to treat it as one.

Three reasons, none fixable with a better system prompt:

  • It is non-deterministic. The same input can produce a different action tomorrow. A boundary that holds 97% of the time is not a boundary; it is a statistic [I think Claude said this, sounds like it :-)]. Security boundaries are supposed to be boring and repeatable, not fun and adventurous.
  • It consumes untrusted text as instructions. Agents read attacker-controlled text all day in READMEs, issues, PR comments, web pages, and tool descriptions, and models fail to reliably separate retrieved data from instructions. The UK NCSC calls LLMs “inherently confusable”; OpenAI and Google both say prompt injection is “unlikely to ever be fully ‘solved’”. Model refusals help [as long as they reject attackers, not defenders, duh!], but they do not hold: in the Nx supply-chain attack, guardrails rejected roughly a quarter of Claude invocations and the attack still succeeded.
  • It cannot police itself (self-review). Asking the actor model whether its own next action is safe is asking the suspect to run the investigation. And you do not need a rogue-AI scenario to see the risk: well-intentioned agents have already wiped production databases at Replit during a declared code freeze and at PocketOS, simply because their judgment failed and their blast radius was too wide. Maybe in the future it will, but not it cannot.

“What about a second model that checks the first?” Simple, beautiful, “secure” model, right?

Independent guard and reviewer models (Google’s Model Armor and the reviewer models OpenAI and Anthropic now ship inside their harnesses, as do many other security vendors) are a real risk-reduction layer, and we recommend them. But a reviewer model is still a probabilistic filter, not a final authorization boundary. You have stacked a second set of preferences on top of the first set: Anthropic’s own reviewer publishes a 17% false-negative rate across 52 real overeager actions. A useful filter, but not a wall, and not “a security invariant” for sure.

The Appsec vs. Firewall Analogy

We have been here before with web applications. Application security (secure coding, input validation, code review) makes the app harder to exploit, but every serious app still ships bugs — so we put runtime boundaries (firewalls, WAFs, OS sandboxes, IAM) around the app to enforce rules it cannot violate even when it is buggy or actively exploited. Agents work the same way:

  • Model alignment, safety training, and prompting ≈ agent “appsec”/modelsec (fewer bad decisions, never zero).
  • The harness ≈ runtime enforcement (sandbox [usually porous], tool policy, and IAM that keep bad decisions from becoming irreversible actions).

👉 The harness is the security boundary for the model, exactly as the firewall and sandbox are boundaries for the app — not because the model is bad, but because software fails.

4. Defense in Depth: Model, Harness, and Gateway

Saying “the harness is the primary execution boundary” does not mean “only the harness matters.” In practice, an enterprise running agents relies on three control layers with distinct jobs:

  • 1. The model (alignment, safety training, refusals). Run by the model vendor to reduce the rate of bad decisions. Probabilistic.
  • 2. The harness (OS sandbox, tool policy, scoped identity, secrets handling, egress allowlist, approval gates, hooks, telemetry). Shipped by the AI vendor and configured by the customer to constrain all execution — both local and remote.
  • 3. The enterprise agentic gateway (policy, identity brokering, MCP proxying, DLP, and logging across external model, tool, and data traffic). Run by the enterprise security team to centralize policy and SOC visibility across agents.
Figure 2. Three control layers — and why local actions bypass the gateway. The harness mediates every proposed action; the enterprise gateway only sees traffic that leaves the endpoint.

The layers are not interchangeable:

  • ❌ A gateway does not see local endpoint execution. If a harness runs as the developer with — dangerously-skip-permissions, the gateway never sees a local rm -rf or secret read on a laptop.
  • ❌ A harness alone does not give the SOC a cross-team control plane.

And the harness is the least mature of the three. The model gets the research attention. The gateway is where enterprise vendors (ours included) are converging. The harness sits in the middle: shipped by AI vendors, configured by developers, treated as a productivity plugin, and mostly invisible to security.

BTW, one of us (Anton) will revisit defense in depth in the age of AI soon (this is one for cloud).

👉 If the harness is the execution boundary, it has to be built, configured, and watched like one.

5. Where the Harness Fails Today

Once you look at the harness as a security boundary rather than a developer convenience, three specific gaps stand out in how harnesses are deployed today.

1. Approval fatigue and bypass modes ( — yolo)
  • A coding agent makes hundreds of tool calls in a single session. Ask a human to approve each one at machine speed and they stop reading within the hour: Anthropic measured users approving 93% of permission prompts before it introduced auto mode. A control that everyone clicks through is not a control.
  • When friction gets too high, developers turn it off, and most major coding-agent harnesses expose an explicit bypass mode for exactly that ( — dangerously-skip-permissions in Claude Code, — yolo in Gemini CLI and Codex).
2. Over-privileged credentials and shared identity
  • Today, local harnesses typically inherit the developer’s ambient git keys, cloud tokens, and MCP connections into Slack, GitHub, and production consoles.
  • Unless sessions carry a separate agent identity, the agent’s blast radius equals the human’s — and the SOC cannot easily tell human and agent apart.
3. The harness itself is an unmonitored software attack surface

Harness CVEs and bypasses

  • Cursor’s MCPoison bound trust to a server’s name rather than its contents (Tenable).
  • A GitHub Copilot exploit used prompt injection to flip on its own auto-approve setting (Embrace The Red).
  • Even actively maintained harnesses ship bugs fast: Anthropic’s claude-code repository lists more than 30 security advisories.

Weaponized configs and flags

  • Agent config files are executable. In June 2026, the Miasma worm planted malicious configs across 73 Microsoft repositories that ran on open. No CVE required.
  • In the Nx attack, which leaked 2,000+ verified secrets, the malware invoked victims’ own AI CLIs with bypass flags to do its reconnaissance.

SOC blindness

  • Harness telemetry is opt-in and redacts prompts and tool arguments by default (Elastic Security Labs).
  • Copilot’s audit log omits local prompts entirely (GitHub).
  • Raw chain-of-thought is never released to customers (Anthropic).

👉 The first two gaps are failures to contain what the agent can do. The third is a failure to protect and monitor the harness itself.

6. How to Secure the Harness: Three Architectural Moves

Closing those gaps means doing two jobs at once:

  • Controlling what the agent can do (security within the harness): enforcing hard limits on execution and reach so a bad model decision cannot become a catastrophe.
  • Protecting the boundary itself (security for the harness): governing the harness’s code, configs, dependencies, and telemetry. A firewall with a remote code execution bug is not a boundary; neither is a harness whose config file can be rewritten by a README.

In practice, that comes down to three architectural moves:

  • Move A: Take enforcement out of the model. Run commands inside an OS sandbox with deterministic tool policy — backed by an independent, reasoning-blind reviewer model for judgment calls (stripped of the actor’s chain-of-thought so the agent cannot talk its way past the check) — with structured steering on blocked actions and human prompts reserved for irreversible ones.
  • Move B: Shrink what the agent can reach. Give the agent its own identity, short-lived scoped tokens, secrets kept outside the sandbox, and an egress allowlist — breaking Simon Willison’s “lethal trifecta” of private data, untrusted content, and an outbound channel.
  • Move C: Govern and watch the harness itself. Put agent config files under branch protection, pin MCP dependencies, and stream action telemetry and hooks to the SIEM.
Figure 3. Where harnesses fail — and the three moves that fix them. Moves A and B contain what the agent can do; Move C governs the harness itself.

Each move gets its own deep dive in Part 2 (hopefully!)

7. What the Harness Cannot Solve (Ever?)

A boundary is only trustworthy if you are honest about where it ends.

  1. Prompt injection at the model layer remains unsolved. That is not a gap in the harness story; it is the premise of it. Every harness control assumes injection can succeed and asks what happens next.
  2. Bugs inside the vendor’s harness are the vendor’s to fix. Pick vendors who publish advisories and ship fixes fast, and treat harness updates like browser updates.
  3. The endpoint remains the thinnest layer. AI detection and response on developer laptops, where most harnesses actually run, is immature. Cloud-hosted sessions sidestep part of this; local agents do not.

In other words, if you endpoints are owned, you need better host security, not “unbeatable” AI security (translation: it will get beaten anyway)

Conclusion & What’s Next

Strip away the new vocabulary and harness security is least privilege, isolation, identity, and logging, applied to a process that reads untrusted text and acts at machine speed. AI changes the speed of the attack, not the fundamentals of defense.

👉 The model will keep having preferences. The harness is where the controls go, and today it is the least watched layer in the stack.

Coming next (hopefully!):

  • Part 2: Three moves to secure the harness. Moves A, B, and C in detail: OS sandboxing and reviewer models (with the error and prompt-reduction rates vendors have published); dedicated identity, scoped tokens, and egress allowlists that break the lethal trifecta; and agent config as code, pinned MCP dependencies, and action telemetry in the SIEM.
  • Part 3: Nobody owns the whole problem. The shared-responsibility split between model providers and enterprises, which vendors ship which control today, the prerequisites that have to be true first, and five actions for this quarter.

Got comments? What stands between a coding agent’s bad decision and your production environment today? If the honest answer is “the model’s judgment,” you have a preference in a place where you need a control.

items.title: Cross-request KV cache exposure in the GLM-5.3 Workers AI model, and our remediation with SGLang
items.summary: On September 8, 2026, we were alerted by a security researcher, Gadi Evron from Knostic, to a tenant isolation issue affecting the GLM-5.3 Workers AI model ( @cf/zai-org/glm-5.3 ) starting on August 27, 2026. We have remediated the issue, and we restored the model on September 9. We have confirmed that no other model hosted on Workers AI was affected. Between August 27 and September 9, a small number of customers using the GLM 5.3 Workers AI model received responses that contained data from other customers' requests made to the same model shortly before theirs. In total, 155 responses were affected, all to prompts longer than 681,280 tokens. After excluding our own testing and the researcher's, the requests we identified are consistent in timing and volume with ordinary long-context use, not with someone repeatedly exploiting the bug. We found no evidence of deliberate exploitation. Today we are publishing this report alongside a post from SGLang, the open-source inference engine that we use, as a coordinated disclosure. This post describes the bug that caused this issue, our response timeline, and the subsequent hardening we have conducted on our production SGLang deployments. We also detail our continued efforts with the upstream maintainers of SGLang to address this and similar bugs. What happened GLM is a text generation model from Z.ai that is built for agentic coding workflows; it is one of the many models available through Workers AI. Gadi Evron submitted a report on September 8 through our HackerOne program stating that very long prompts sent to @cf/zai-org/glm-5.3 on Workers AI sometimes returned text that belonged to other users' sessions. Cloudflare reproduced the issue the next morning and took the model offline within 40 minutes of declaring an incident. We then deployed a corrected configuration and a patched inference engine, and restored service the same day. This specific report of cross-request KV cache exposure was the result of two overlapping issues. The first was a misconfiguration of the open-source inference engine, SGLang, used by Cloudflare. We deployed GLM 5.3 with a 1,048,576-token context window, but the KV cache pool on our prefill GPUs only had room for 681,280 tokens. We were aware of this mismatch before launch. We expected the engine to return an error for any prompt it could not process, and our long-context tests returned successful responses, so we did not believe this to be an issue. The second was a bug in how SGLang handled the resulting over-length requests in disaggregated prefill/decode mode. A prompt that did not fit the pool was internally marked as rejected and replaced with a one-token placeholder, but instead of aborting the request and returning a client error, prefill generated the KV cache for the placeholder prompt and transferred it to the decode node. The decode node received a "transfer complete" message and assumed that prefill overwrote the KV cache from previous requests with the full prompt for this request, when in fact it left the majority of the previous state intact. The decode node subsequently generated a response while attending over stale cache pages that still held data from earlier requests. As a result, responses to prompts longer than 681,280 tokens could contain data from other users' GLM 5.3 sessions. Immediate remediation After disabling the model , we took the following actions to correct this vulnerability before restoring public access to it: To fix our configuration, we made the pool hold the full context. We adjusted our GLM 5.3 configuration to match our GLM 5.2 configuration, which freed enough GPU memory that the prefill KV pool now holds about 2.04 million tokens, roughly twice the 1,048,576-token context length. A prompt that fits the context window now always fits the pool, so the rejection path is never reached for a valid request. This alone prevents the bug from being exercised. To fix the engine, we also made the rejection path safe. Relying on pool size alone is fragile: any change to quantization, tensor parallelism, CUDA graph sizes, or a future model version changes the pool size in a way that's easy to miss. Furthermore, there may be other situations in which the prefill scheduler can reject a request and trigger the same bug. To prevent this, we also patched the engine so that a request carrying a pending rejection is retired at the disaggregation admission queue, with its original error, before any bootstrap, allocation, or KV transfer happens. We proposed this upstream as #38704 , which also had the decode node verify that the number of tokens transferred matches the number it reserved. The fix was already on SGLang main in #36988 , merged September 6 for a related failure path but not yet released. The maintainers also merged #38935 , which rejects these requests earlier, following our approach. We validated both changes against the researcher's reproduction script and our own canary-marker tests before restoring the model. We have written about this architecture before in our posts on high-performance LLMs and smaller, faster, safer models . The KV cache in GPU memory is a shared pool of fixed-size pages. Each request is assigned pages when it is admitted and releases them when it finishes. Pages are not currently zeroed between requests; the next request that gets a page simply overwrites it. This approach is common among inference engines and is necessary to achieve the best performance, but it means that the inference engine is responsible for tracking ownership of these memory pages. KV cache page ownership and lifetime tracking has to deal with not just shared ownership within a node (KV cache offload and token generation both access the memory with different lifetimes), but also ownership that is technically shared with the remote prefill node (which holds a simultaneous mutable reference to the page). Furthermore, the size of this pool is not a configuration value. SGLang sizes it at startup from whatever GPU memory remains after loading the model weights. The model's advertised context length is a separate configuration value. Nothing forces the two to agree, and it is our job to check that they do. When a prompt arrived that was longer than the KV pool could hold, SGLang's scheduler rejected it. Prefill sent one page of KV to decode and signaled that the transfer was complete. Decode admission. Decode's admission queue had the same finished() check, so it accepted the handoff. Decode attention. Decode started generating and attention read all 8 reserved pages. Only page P0 had been written by this request. Pages P1 to P7 still held what earlier requests left in them: other users' prompts and partial generations. Response. The client got HTTP 200 instead of HTTP 400. prompt_tokens matched the long prompt and the reply was coherent. Every other disaggregated deployment on Workers AI has KV pools larger than its context length on both prefill and decode, so no request could reach the rejection path. We built a prototype of this over the summer and described it in August . In our tests it cost under 1% in throughput and tail latency. We tested it on GLM 5.2 in mid-August, but disabled it shortly afterwards due to reliability issues. The prototype was also tied to specific attention backends and model architectures, so it could not be a general fix. We are working with the SGLang team to build a production version into the engine that works across every model, rather than maintaining Cloudflare-specific patches. The per-transfer checksum in #39500 is a first step: it validates the handoff from prefill to decode. Page-level tags go further, because they check every read, including reads long after the transfer. Integrity by mathematical impossibility RDMA copies data directly from one node’s memory to another’s. It’s vital for the two machines to agree on where the data goes, how large it is, and when it’s finished; any mismatch can cause the receiver to read the wrong data. This bug is an example of a consistency failure in a distributed system, in which the two machines had inconsistent views of the state of that system. Elsewhere in Cloudflare, we have put effort into proving the safety of distributed systems using formal verification methods. Topaz enables conflict-free IP selection for our authoritative DNS servers. Models of Meerkat’s QuePaxa implementation have demonstrated consistency bugs that were subsequently fixed. We are now directing our experience in formal methods to KV cache transfer engines. This will start with modeling and proving the safety of an RDMA-based KV cache transfer protocol. The goal is to model our production SGLang’s distributed KV cache system using Mooncake, then track and fix any divergence from the safety properties we want to guarantee. The aim is to prove — as far as possible — that a bug like this cannot occur again. Realistically, we expect gaps in what the provers can tell us, but proving the rest of the system allows us to more closely review and monitor those gaps. We want to thank the researcher, Gadi Evron, who reported this through our HackerOne program with a clear, reproducible script and gave us time to fix it and to coordinate with the SGLang maintainers before publishing. We also want to thank the SGLang team at RadixArk, who treated this as their problem as well as ours and landed the upstream fixes with urgency.
items.summary_html:
On September 8, 2026, we were alerted by a security researcher, Gadi Evron from Knostic, to a tenant isolation issue affecting the GLM-5.3 Workers AI model (@cf/zai-org/glm-5.3) starting on August 27, 2026. We have remediated the issue, and we restored the model on September 9. We have confirmed that no other model hosted on Workers AI was affected.

Between August 27 and September 9, a small number of customers using the GLM 5.3 Workers AI model received responses that contained data from other customers' requests made to the same model shortly before theirs. In total, 155 responses were affected, all to prompts longer than 681,280 tokens.

After excluding our own testing and the researcher's, the requests we identified are consistent in timing and volume with ordinary long-context use, not with someone repeatedly exploiting the bug. We found no evidence of deliberate exploitation.

Today we are publishing this report alongside a post from SGLang, the open-source inference engine that we use, as a coordinated disclosure. This post describes the bug that caused this issue, our response timeline, and the subsequent hardening we have conducted on our production SGLang deployments. We also detail our continued efforts with the upstream maintainers of SGLang to address this and similar bugs.

What happened

GLM is a text generation model from Z.ai that is built for agentic coding workflows; it is one of the many models available through Workers AI. Gadi Evron submitted a report on September 8 through our HackerOne program stating that very long prompts sent to @cf/zai-org/glm-5.3 on Workers AI sometimes returned text that belonged to other users' sessions. Cloudflare reproduced the issue the next morning and took the model offline within 40 minutes of declaring an incident. We then deployed a corrected configuration and a patched inference engine, and restored service the same day.  

This specific report of cross-request KV cache exposure was the result of two overlapping issues. The first was a misconfiguration of the open-source inference engine, SGLang, used by Cloudflare. We deployed GLM 5.3 with a 1,048,576-token context window, but the KV cache pool on our prefill GPUs only had room for 681,280 tokens. We were aware of this mismatch before launch. We expected the engine to return an error for any prompt it could not process, and our long-context tests returned successful responses, so we did not believe this to be an issue.

The second was a bug in how SGLang handled the resulting over-length requests in disaggregated prefill/decode mode. A prompt that did not fit the pool was internally marked as rejected and replaced with a one-token placeholder, but instead of aborting the request and returning a client error, prefill generated the KV cache for the placeholder prompt and transferred it to the decode node. The decode node received a "transfer complete" message and assumed that prefill overwrote the KV cache from previous requests with the full prompt for this request, when in fact it left the majority of the previous state intact. The decode node subsequently generated a response while attending over stale cache pages that still held data from earlier requests. As a result, responses to prompts longer than 681,280 tokens could contain data from other users' GLM 5.3 sessions.

Immediate remediation

After disabling the model, we took the following actions to correct this vulnerability before restoring public access to it:

To fix our configuration, we made the pool hold the full context. We adjusted our GLM 5.3 configuration to match our GLM 5.2 configuration, which freed enough GPU memory that the prefill KV pool now holds about 2.04 million tokens, roughly twice the 1,048,576-token context length. A prompt that fits the context window now always fits the pool, so the rejection path is never reached for a valid request. This alone prevents the bug from being exercised.

To fix the engine, we also made the rejection path safe. Relying on pool size alone is fragile: any change to quantization, tensor parallelism, CUDA graph sizes, or a future model version changes the pool size in a way that's easy to miss. Furthermore, there may be other situations in which the prefill scheduler can reject a request and trigger the same bug. To prevent this, we also patched the engine so that a request carrying a pending rejection is retired at the disaggregation admission queue, with its original error, before any bootstrap, allocation, or KV transfer happens. We proposed this upstream as #38704, which also had the decode node verify that the number of tokens transferred matches the number it reserved. The fix was already on SGLang main in #36988, merged September 6 for a related failure path but not yet released. The maintainers also merged #38935, which rejects these requests earlier, following our approach.

We validated both changes against the researcher's reproduction script and our own canary-marker tests before restoring the model.

Background: how we serve GLM 5.3

Workers AI runs GLM 5.3 with SGLang in a disaggregated configuration: a pool of prefill GPUs processes the prompt and produces the model's KV cache for it, then hands that cache over remote direct memory access (RDMA), via Mooncake, to a pool of decode GPUs that generate the response. We have written about this architecture before in our posts on high-performance LLMs and smaller, faster, safer models.

The KV cache in GPU memory is a shared pool of fixed-size pages. Each request is assigned pages when it is admitted and releases them when it finishes. Pages are not currently zeroed between requests; the next request that gets a page simply overwrites it. This approach is common among inference engines and is necessary to achieve the best performance, but it means that the inference engine is responsible for tracking ownership of these memory pages. KV cache page ownership and lifetime tracking has to deal with not just shared ownership within a node (KV cache offload and token generation both access the memory with different lifetimes), but also ownership that is technically shared with the remote prefill node (which holds a simultaneous mutable reference to the page).

Furthermore, the size of this pool is not a configuration value. SGLang sizes it at startup from whatever GPU memory remains after loading the model weights. The model's advertised context length is a separate configuration value. Nothing forces the two to agree, and it is our job to check that they do.

Issue one: misconfiguration

On our GLM 5.3 prefill nodes with our configuration, the pool came to 681,280 tokens while the model's context length is 1,048,576 tokens. The selected KV pool size is printed by SGLang in logs during startup and exposed as a metric. We were aware of this size mismatch; however, during pre-launch testing we observed successful HTTP status codes and a streaming body with no error frames during benchmarking. We assumed that the engine was capable of gracefully handling the difference between the KV cache pool and requested context window via streaming or some other mechanism.

This was one critical gap in our testing: we only validated HTTP response codes and engine performance at long contexts, without validating model output and coherence. We now check KV pool size against context length directly, from the running engine, before any disaggregated deployment change ships, rather than inferring it from response codes.

Issue two: SGLang bug

In v0.5.21, the SGLang team has now addressed this bug in how it was handling prompts longer than the KV pool size. Here’s what was happening before.

When a prompt arrived that was longer than the KV pool could hold, SGLang's scheduler rejected it. The rejection path (Req.set_finish_with_abort) recorded the error to be returned to the client and swapped the prompt for a one-token placeholder so that the request could drain through the normal batch machinery without allocating real memory. On a single-node deployment this worked: the placeholder ran, the batch finished, and the client received an error.

In disaggregated mode such as we operate, the admission queues on both prefill and decode checked whether a request was finished, not whether it was rejected. A rejected request reported itself as live. So:

  1. Bootstrap. The router told the decode node the prompt length (8 pages in the diagram). Decode reserved 8 KV pages for the request.
  2. Prefill admission. The prefill admission queue admitted any request where req.finished() was False. A rejected request stored its rejection in to_finish, not finished_reason, so finished() still returned False. The rejected request was admitted.
  3. Prefill forward pass. Rejection had already replaced the prompt with a one-token placeholder. Prefill ran a trivial forward pass on that one token.
  4. KV transfer. Prefill sent one page of KV to decode and signaled that the transfer was complete.
  5. Decode admission. Decode's admission queue had the same finished() check, so it accepted the handoff.
  6. Decode attention. Decode started generating and attention read all 8 reserved pages. Only page P0 had been written by this request. Pages P1 to P7 still held what earlier requests left in them: other users' prompts and partial generations.
  7. Response. The client got HTTP 200 instead of HTTP 400. prompt_tokens matched the long prompt and the reply was coherent. It arrived faster than an 8-page prefill should take, and it contained content from other users' KV pages.

Every request over the threshold behaved this way. This bug had been reported to SGLang by another user as issue #30233 on July 6, 2026, which Cloudflare noticed while investigating this incident. We had been flagging these types of issues with SGLang since v0.5.10 and this security incident sped up work that Cloudflare had already started in collaboration with the SGLang team. The patch for this issue was released in SGLang v0.5.20, with follow-ups in v0.5.21 and v0.5.22, and is available for all other operators dependent on SGLang to use. We highly recommend all operators update SGLang dependencies to v0.5.22 or later. For more details on specific PRs, read on below.

GLM 5.3 was the only model affected by this bug. Every other disaggregated deployment on Workers AI has KV pools larger than its context length on both prefill and decode, so no request could reach the rejection path. We have applied the engine fix and the hardening described below to every model we serve with SGLang, and our deployment checks require them for every new deployment.

Holds pages on every transfer failure, not only decode-initiated aborts.

Race

#41618

v0.5.21

Fixes a regression in the abort notification path.

Race

#43719

v0.5.22

A failed Mooncake send no longer reports its writes as drained.

Race

#37077

v0.5.22

Tags abort messages per request so a reused ID cannot consume a stale confirmation. Adds MORI support.

Race

#36612

v0.5.20

Shares the prefill-to-decode failure notification across Mooncake, NIXL, and MORI.

Race

#32758

v0.5.20

Optional cap on Mooncake transfer batch size, so one timed-out call cannot leave an unbounded number of writes in flight.

Lifetime

#30899

v0.5.21

Decode waits for an in-progress offload to host memory before retracting a request and freeing its pages. Authored by Cloudflare.

Lifetime

#43562

v0.5.22

Keeps tensor-parallel ranks in agreement when a host-memory cache restore fails.

Observability

#39500

v0.5.21

Adds --disaggregation-enable-kv-checksum: decode verifies a checksum of the transferred KV before generating. Cleanup in #39729, merged and awaiting release.

Observability

#38596, #40642

v0.5.20, v0.5.21

Fixes for SGLang's KV canary, which detects and logs potential corruption.

Observability

#41128

v0.5.22

Metrics for deferred release: count, duration, and whether each hold ended on drain confirmation or timeout.

These follow-ups are still works in progress:

  • #39729 Additional cleanup for --disaggregation-enable-kv-checksum. Merged, awaiting release.
  • Zero KV pages on release, draft proposal: #46435
  • Extend KV checksum validation from the prefill-to-decode handoff to every decode step (see Integrity by construction, below)
  • Broader KV Canary and KV Checksum model and feature support
What we recommend to other operators

If you run SGLang in disaggregated prefill/decode mode, we recommend the following:

  1. Measure your KV pool and compare it to your context length, on every prefill and decode node, from the engine's startup log, after every change to weights, quantization, parallelism, or memory fraction. If the pool is smaller, lower the context length to fit. Do not rely on a proxy to enforce the limit, and do not assume the engine will reject what does not fit. This is the check we did not enforce.
  2. Upgrade to a build that includes #36988 and #38935 (v0.5.22 or later), so an over-length request is rejected before handoff regardless of pool size. This is the engine-side fix, and it is the backstop for the day your check in step one is wrong.
  3. Run with deferred KV release on both roles (default after #41023), and bound your Mooncake transfer batches so a single timed-out call cannot leave an unbounded tail of writes.
  4. Turn on corruption detection where your model supports it. --disaggregation-enable-kv-checksum and --kv-canary do not yet cover every model architecture. Check your logs to confirm requests are being verified. We are working with the SGLang team to extend both checks to more architectures, including GLM 5.3, GLM 5.3 Flash, and DeepSeek V4.
  5. Ensure your proxy is not generating unnecessary aborts. Configure your load balancer to allow requests to proceed up to the first token, so that you do not trigger an abort that requires cross-node coordination.
Longer termIntegrity by construction

Configuration checks and lifecycle fixes reduce the number of ways a page can be misused. They do not make misuse impossible, and this incident is a reminder that the next bug will have a shape we have not seen. The durable answer is for the engine to detect, at read time, that a request is about to attend over a page it does not own, and fail that one request rather than return someone else's data.

We built a prototype of this over the summer and described it in August. Every physical KV page carries a tag that changes when the page is reallocated, each request records the tags it expects, and the mapping is checked before decode reads the cache. In our tests it cost under 1% in throughput and tail latency. We tested it on GLM 5.2 in mid-August, but disabled it shortly afterwards due to reliability issues.

The prototype was also tied to specific attention backends and model architectures, so it could not be a general fix. We are working with the SGLang team to build a production version into the engine that works across every model, rather than maintaining Cloudflare-specific patches. The per-transfer checksum in #39500 is a first step: it validates the handoff from prefill to decode. Page-level tags go further, because they check every read, including reads long after the transfer.

Integrity by mathematical impossibility

RDMA copies data directly from one node’s memory to another’s. It’s vital for the two machines to agree on where the data goes, how large it is, and when it’s finished; any mismatch can cause the receiver to read the wrong data. This bug is an example of a consistency failure in a distributed system, in which the two machines had inconsistent views of the state of that system.

Elsewhere in Cloudflare, we have put effort into proving the safety of distributed systems using formal verification methods. Topaz enables conflict-free IP selection for our authoritative DNS servers. Models of Meerkat’s QuePaxa implementation have demonstrated consistency bugs that were subsequently fixed.

We are now directing our experience in formal methods to KV cache transfer engines. This will start with modeling and proving the safety of an RDMA-based KV cache transfer protocol. The goal is to model our production SGLang’s distributed KV cache system using Mooncake, then track and fix any divergence from the safety properties we want to guarantee. The aim is to prove — as far as possible — that a bug like this cannot occur again. Realistically, we expect gaps in what the provers can tell us, but proving the rest of the system allows us to more closely review and monitor those gaps.

Coordinated disclosure

We are publishing this report as part of a coordinated disclosure. We want to thank the researcher, Gadi Evron, who reported this through our HackerOne program with a clear, reproducible script and gave us time to fix it and to coordinate with the SGLang maintainers before publishing. We also want to thank the SGLang team at RadixArk, who treated this as their problem as well as ours and landed the upstream fixes with urgency.

Read more at the post from the SGLang team.

If you find a security issue in Workers AI, please report it at hackerone.com/cloudflare.
