items.summary: Written in collaboration with Gunjan Jain​ and yuvalpery​ As described in our earlier blog, Addressing PHP2Shell CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619: upgrade guidance and Azure WAF mitigations , we strongly recommend upgrading to a patched version of PHP as soon as possible. Upgrading PHP remains the recommended and complete remediation for these vulnerabilities. For customers who are unable to upgrade immediately, this guidance provides WAF custom rules that can help reduce exposure to selected request patterns associated with exploitation techniques for these vulnerabilities. WAF custom rules The following three custom rules can be considered based on your application configuration and traffic patterns. Because custom rules can affect legitimate application traffic, review the potential application impact and validate the rules before enabling enforcement. Restrict PHP session upload progress PHP supports session upload progress for tracking file uploads. For applications that do not depend on this functionality, customers can use a custom rule to restrict multipart form requests containing PHP_SESSION_UPLOAD_PROGRESS. The rule checks for multipart/form-data requests whose inspected request body contains the PHP session upload progress token. Custom rule definitions: Azure Front Door WAF { "name": "BlockPhpSessionUploadProgress", "priority": 100, "enabledState": "Enabled", "ruleType": "MatchRule", "action": "Block", "matchConditions": [ { "matchVariable": "RequestHeader", "selector": "Content-Type", "operator": "Contains", "negateCondition": false, "transforms": ["Lowercase"], "matchValue": ["multipart/form-data"] }, { "matchVariable": "RequestBody", "operator": "Contains", "negateCondition": false, "matchValue": ["php_session_upload_progress"], "transforms": ["Lowercase"] } ] } Application Gateway and Application Gateway for Container (AGC) WAF { "name": "BlockPhpSessionUploadProgress", "priority": 90, "ruleType": "MatchRule", "action": "Block", "state": "Enabled", "matchConditions": [ { "matchVariables": [ { "variableName": "RequestHeaders", "selector": "Content-Type" } ], "operator": "Contains", "negationConditon": false, "matchValues": [ "multipart/form-data" ], "transforms": [ "Lowercase" ] }, { "matchVariables": [ { "variableName": "PostArgs" } ], "operator": "Contains", "negationConditon": false, "matchValues": [ "php_session_upload_progress" ], "transforms": [ "Lowercase" ] } ] } This rule reduces exposure through the PHP session-upload-progress path but does not address all exploitation paths associated with the vulnerabilities. Potential application impact: Applications that legitimately use PHP session upload progress will also match this rule. A substring match may also detect the token when it appears as harmless text or in uploaded content exposed to inspection. Limit deeply nested form parameters Customers can use a custom rule to identify unusually deep parameter nesting in application/x-www-form-urlencoded requests. The proposed rule detects request field names containing 20 or more levels of bracket nesting after URL decoding. Because the 20-level threshold is an application policy choice rather than a vulnerability-defined boundary, legitimate applications using deeply nested parameters may also match this rule. Custom rule definitions: Azure Front Door WAF: { "name": "PhpFormNesting20", "priority": 110, "enabledState": "Enabled", "ruleType": "MatchRule", "action": "Log", "matchConditions": [ { "matchVariable": "RequestHeader", "selector": "Content-Type", "operator": "BeginsWith", "negateCondition": false, "transforms": [ "Trim", "Lowercase" ], "matchValue": [ "application/x-www-form-urlencoded" ] }, { "matchVariable": "RequestBody", "operator": "RegEx", "negateCondition": false, "transforms": [ "UrlDecode" ], "matchValue": [ "(?:^|&)[^&=\\[]+(?:\\[[^&=\\]]*\\]){20}" ] } ] } Application Gateway and Application Gateway for Container (AGC) WAF { "name": "PhpFormNesting20", "priority": 91, "ruleType": "MatchRule", "action": "Log", "state": "Enabled", "matchConditions": [ { "matchVariables": [ { "variableName": "RequestHeaders", "selector": "Content-Type" } ], "operator": "BeginsWith", "negationConditon": false, "matchValues": [ "application/x-www-form-urlencoded" ], "transforms": [ "Trim", "Lowercase" ] }, { "matchVariables": [ { "variableName": "RequestBody" } ], "operator": "Regex", "negationConditon": false, "matchValues": [ "(?:^|&)[^&=\\[]+(?:\\[[^&=\\]]*\\]){20}" ], "transforms": [ "UrlDecode" ] } ] } Recommended deployment: Start with the rule in Log mode and review matches against legitimate application traffic. Consider moving the rule to Block only after validating application compatibility. Limit deeply nested multipart parameters Customers can apply a similar control to multipart/form-data requests by detecting deeply nested field names. The proposed rule detects multipart field names containing 20 or more levels of nesting where the relevant request content is available to WAF inspection. As with deeply nested URL-encoded parameters, legitimate applications may use complex multipart field structures. Custom rule definitions: Azure Front Door WAF { "name": "PhpMultipartNesting20", "priority": 111, "enabledState": "Enabled", "ruleType": "MatchRule", "action": "Log", "matchConditions": [ { "matchVariable": "RequestHeader", "selector": "Content-Type", "operator": "BeginsWith", "negateCondition": false, "transforms": [ "Trim", "Lowercase" ], "matchValue": [ "multipart/form-data" ] }, { "matchVariable": "RequestBody", "operator": "RegEx", "negateCondition": false, "matchValue": [ "(?i)(?:^|\\r?\\n)content-disposition:[ \\t]*form-data[^\\r\\n]*;[ \\t]*name[ \\t]*=[ \\t]*(?:\"(?:\\\\[\"\\\\]|[^\"\\r\\n\\[])+(?:\\[(?:\\\\[\"\\\\]|[^\"\\r\\n\\]])*\\]){20}|[^ \\t\\r\\n;\"\\[]+(?:\\[[^ \\t\\r\\n;\"\\]]*\\]){20})" ] } ] } Application Gateway and Application Gateway for Container (AGC) WAF { "name": "PhpMultipartNesting20", "priority": 92, "ruleType": "MatchRule", "action": "Log", "state": "Enabled", "matchConditions": [ { "matchVariables": [ { "variableName": "RequestHeaders", "selector": "Content-Type" } ], "operator": "BeginsWith", "negationConditon": false, "matchValues": [ "multipart/form-data" ], "transforms": [ "Trim", "Lowercase" ] }, { "matchVariables": [ { "variableName": "PostArgs" } ], "operator": "Regex", "negationConditon": false, "matchValues": [ "^[^\\[\\]]+(?:\\[[^\\]]*\\]){20}" ], "transforms": [] } ] } This rule targets deeply nested multipart field names. It does not restrict every multipart upload or provide complete mitigation for the underlying vulnerabilities. Recommended deployment: Start in Log mode, review matching traffic, and consider moving to Block only after validating the impact on your application. Deployment and validation considerations We recommend applying these custom rules only to affected PHP application domains and routes, including extensionless routes handled by PHP, rather than broadly applying them to unrelated applications. Before enabling enforcement: Review the potential impact on legitimate application traffic. Test each custom rule independently before deploying the rules together. Start applicable rules in Log mode and review legitimate matches. Verify the WAF policy scope and custom-rule precedence. After changing a rule to Block , validate both application behavior and the corresponding WAF events. Continue to prioritize upgrading PHP even when these controls are deployed. Custom rules may produce false positives, and WAF request-body inspection boundaries can affect coverage. An earlier terminal Allow rule in the WAF policy can also bypass subsequent custom-rule checks. The custom rules described above target selected request patterns associated with exploitation techniques for CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619 . They reduce selected attack surfaces but do not provide complete protection against either vulnerability. You can find more information about Custom Rules on Azure WAF for Application Gateway here or for Azure Front Door here . Upgrading to a patched version of PHP remains the recommended and complete remediation.
items.summary_html:
Written in collaboration with Gunjan Jain​ and yuvalpery​ 

As described in our earlier blog, Addressing PHP2Shell CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619: upgrade guidance and Azure WAF mitigations, we strongly recommend upgrading to a patched version of PHP as soon as possible. Upgrading PHP remains the recommended and complete remediation for these vulnerabilities. 

For customers who are unable to upgrade immediately, this guidance provides WAF custom rules that can help reduce exposure to selected request patterns associated with exploitation techniques for these vulnerabilities.  

WAF custom rules 

The following three custom rules can be considered based on your application configuration and traffic patterns. Because custom rules can affect legitimate application traffic, review the potential application impact and validate the rules before enabling enforcement. 

Restrict PHP session upload progress

PHP supports session upload progress for tracking file uploads. For applications that do not depend on this functionality, customers can use a custom rule to restrict multipart form requests containing PHP_SESSION_UPLOAD_PROGRESS. 

The rule checks for multipart/form-data requests whose inspected request body contains the PHP session upload progress token. 

Custom rule definitions:

Azure Front Door WAF

{    "name": "BlockPhpSessionUploadProgress",    "priority": 100,    "enabledState": "Enabled",    "ruleType": "MatchRule",    "action": "Block",    "matchConditions": [      {         "matchVariable": "RequestHeader",         "selector": "Content-Type",         "operator": "Contains",         "negateCondition": false,         "transforms": ["Lowercase"],         "matchValue": ["multipart/form-data"]       },       {         "matchVariable": "RequestBody",         "operator": "Contains",         "negateCondition": false,         "matchValue": ["php_session_upload_progress"],         "transforms": ["Lowercase"]       }    ]  }

Application Gateway and Application Gateway for Container (AGC) WAF 

{ "name": "BlockPhpSessionUploadProgress", "priority": 90, "ruleType": "MatchRule", "action": "Block", "state": "Enabled", "matchConditions": [ { "matchVariables": [ { "variableName": "RequestHeaders", "selector": "Content-Type" } ], "operator": "Contains", "negationConditon": false, "matchValues": [ "multipart/form-data" ], "transforms": [ "Lowercase" ] }, { "matchVariables": [ { "variableName": "PostArgs" } ], "operator": "Contains", "negationConditon": false, "matchValues": [ "php_session_upload_progress" ], "transforms": [ "Lowercase" ] } ] }

This rule reduces exposure through the PHP session-upload-progress path but does not address all exploitation paths associated with the vulnerabilities. 

Potential application impact: Applications that legitimately use PHP session upload progress will also match this rule. A substring match may also detect the token when it appears as harmless text or in uploaded content exposed to inspection.

Limit deeply nested form parameters

Customers can use a custom rule to identify unusually deep parameter nesting in application/x-www-form-urlencoded requests. 

The proposed rule detects request field names containing 20 or more levels of bracket nesting after URL decoding. 

Because the 20-level threshold is an application policy choice rather than a vulnerability-defined boundary, legitimate applications using deeply nested parameters may also match this rule. 

Custom rule definitions:

Azure Front Door WAF: 

{    "name": "PhpFormNesting20",    "priority": 110,    "enabledState": "Enabled",    "ruleType": "MatchRule",    "action": "Log",    "matchConditions": [      {        "matchVariable": "RequestHeader",        "selector": "Content-Type",        "operator": "BeginsWith",        "negateCondition": false,        "transforms": [          "Trim",          "Lowercase"        ],        "matchValue": [          "application/x-www-form-urlencoded"        ]      },      {        "matchVariable": "RequestBody",        "operator": "RegEx",        "negateCondition": false,        "transforms": [          "UrlDecode"        ],        "matchValue": [          "(?:^|&)[^&=\\[]+(?:\\[[^&=\\]]*\\]){20}"        ]      }    ]  } 

Application Gateway and Application Gateway for Container (AGC) WAF 

{ "name": "PhpFormNesting20", "priority": 91, "ruleType": "MatchRule", "action": "Log", "state": "Enabled", "matchConditions": [ { "matchVariables": [ { "variableName": "RequestHeaders", "selector": "Content-Type" } ], "operator": "BeginsWith", "negationConditon": false, "matchValues": [ "application/x-www-form-urlencoded" ], "transforms": [ "Trim", "Lowercase" ] }, { "matchVariables": [ { "variableName": "RequestBody" } ], "operator": "Regex", "negationConditon": false, "matchValues": [ "(?:^|&)[^&=\\[]+(?:\\[[^&=\\]]*\\]){20}" ], "transforms": [ "UrlDecode" ] } ] }

Recommended deployment: Start with the rule in Log mode and review matches against legitimate application traffic. Consider moving the rule to Block only after validating application compatibility. 

Limit deeply nested multipart parameters

Customers can apply a similar control to multipart/form-data requests by detecting deeply nested field names. 

The proposed rule detects multipart field names containing 20 or more levels of nesting where the relevant request content is available to WAF inspection. 

As with deeply nested URL-encoded parameters, legitimate applications may use complex multipart field structures. 

Custom rule definitions:

Azure Front Door WAF

{    "name": "PhpMultipartNesting20",    "priority": 111,    "enabledState": "Enabled",    "ruleType": "MatchRule",    "action": "Log",    "matchConditions": [      {        "matchVariable": "RequestHeader",        "selector": "Content-Type",        "operator": "BeginsWith",        "negateCondition": false,        "transforms": [          "Trim",          "Lowercase"        ],        "matchValue": [          "multipart/form-data"        ]      },      {        "matchVariable": "RequestBody",        "operator": "RegEx",        "negateCondition": false,        "matchValue": [          "(?i)(?:^|\\r?\\n)content-disposition:[ \\t]*form-data[^\\r\\n]*;[ \\t]*name[ \\t]*=[ \\t]*(?:\"(?:\\\\[\"\\\\]|[^\"\\r\\n\\[])+(?:\\[(?:\\\\[\"\\\\]|[^\"\\r\\n\\]])*\\]){20}|[^ \\t\\r\\n;\"\\[]+(?:\\[[^ \\t\\r\\n;\"\\]]*\\]){20})"        ]      }    ]  } 

Application Gateway and Application Gateway for Container (AGC) WAF 

{ "name": "PhpMultipartNesting20", "priority": 92, "ruleType": "MatchRule", "action": "Log", "state": "Enabled", "matchConditions": [ { "matchVariables": [ { "variableName": "RequestHeaders", "selector": "Content-Type" } ], "operator": "BeginsWith", "negationConditon": false, "matchValues": [ "multipart/form-data" ], "transforms": [ "Trim", "Lowercase" ] }, { "matchVariables": [ { "variableName": "PostArgs" } ], "operator": "Regex", "negationConditon": false, "matchValues": [ "^[^\\[\\]]+(?:\\[[^\\]]*\\]){20}" ], "transforms": [] } ] }

This rule targets deeply nested multipart field names. It does not restrict every multipart upload or provide complete mitigation for the underlying vulnerabilities. 

Recommended deployment: Start in Log mode, review matching traffic, and consider moving to Block only after validating the impact on your application. 

Deployment and validation considerations

We recommend applying these custom rules only to affected PHP application domains and routes, including extensionless routes handled by PHP, rather than broadly applying them to unrelated applications. 

Before enabling enforcement: 

  • Review the potential impact on legitimate application traffic. 
  • Test each custom rule independently before deploying the rules together. 
  • Start applicable rules in Log mode and review legitimate matches. 
  • Verify the WAF policy scope and custom-rule precedence. 
  • After changing a rule to Block, validate both application behavior and the corresponding WAF events. 
  • Continue to prioritize upgrading PHP even when these controls are deployed. 

Custom rules may produce false positives, and WAF request-body inspection boundaries can affect coverage. An earlier terminal Allow rule in the WAF policy can also bypass subsequent custom-rule checks. 

The custom rules described above target selected request patterns associated with exploitation techniques for CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619. They reduce selected attack surfaces but do not provide complete protection against either vulnerability. 

You can find more information about Custom Rules on Azure WAF for Application Gateway here or for Azure Front Door here.  

Upgrading to a patched version of PHP remains the recommended and complete remediation.

items.title: Addressing PHP2Shell CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619: upgrade guidance and Azure WAF mitigations
items.summary: Written in collaboration with yuvalpery​ and Gunjan Jain​ Introduction Today, two critical remote code execution (RCE) vulnerabilities were disclosed in PHP. We strongly recommend that customers upgrade to a patched version of PHP as soon as possible. Upgrading is the only way to fully remediate these vulnerabilities. Read more on the PHP official website. Microsoft has been part of the coordinated industry response to these vulnerabilities, working alongside the PHP Foundation, Wiz, security researchers, and other industry partners to help protect customers. Azure Web Application Firewall (WAF) has developed mitigations against known exploitation patterns to provide an additional layer of protection while customers apply the PHP security updates. These protections are intended to complement patching and are not a replacement for it. About the vulnerabilities: CVE-2026-109618 - RCE via OOM corruption CVE-2026-109619 - RCE via stale global state Both vulnerabilities can be exploited over the network without privileges or user interaction, with a high potential impact on confidentiality, integrity, and availability. The vulnerabilities relate to PHP handling of memory when a request terminates abnormally, for example due to memory exhaustion or a fatal error. Under certain conditions, improper memory handling could allow an attacker to achieve remote code execution. Fixed versions: 8.5.12, 8.4.27, 8.3.36, 8.2.35. Refer to vendor guidance for patching of different versions of PHP. Recommended action: upgrade PHP We recommend that customers: Upgrade all PHP deployments to a patched version, including virtual machines, containers, base images , and platform runtimes. We suggest prioritizing internet-facing workloads. Rebuild and redeploy container images that include their own PHP runtime, since updating the host does not update PHP inside an image. Migrate to a supported PHP branch if the branch currently in use no longer receives security fixes. Treat the Azure WAF mitigations below as a temporary, supplementary measure. They address a specific technique and do not remediate the underlying vulnerabilities. Azure WAF protection If you are unable to upgrade PHP to a patched version immediately, apply the following mitigations in the interim - Azure Front Door WAF: Apply the mitigation using custom rules for request-side mitigation and enable the managed rule for response-side mitigation. Application Gateway WAF: Apply the mitigation using custom rules for request-side mitigation and enable the rewrite rule for response-side mitigation. Application Gateway for Container WAF: Apply the mitigation using custom rules for request-side mitigation. See below sections for details. Mitigation using custom rules These custom rules can help reduce exposure to selected request patterns associated with exploitation techniques for these vulnerabilities. Depending on application traffic, the rules may result in false positives and affect legitimate requests. They are intended as temporary mitigations and do not replace the need to upgrade PHP. Learn more: Azure WAF custom rules for PHP2Shell mitigation. Request-side signals alone may not be sufficient to reliably identify certain exploitation attempts. Signals in the server response can provide additional evidence that malicious activity has occurred, enabling more targeted mitigation with higher confidence and lower false positives. For this vulnerability, Azure WAF identifies known malicious patterns in the session and removes the potentially malicious elements from the response before it reaches the client. This provides an additional layer of protection for supported exploitation scenarios, while patching PHP remains necessary to fully address the underlying vulnerability. Azure Front Door WAF: managed rule A managed rule to handle potential attack vector in response is currently rolling out for Azure Front Door WAF, expected to complete October 28. Once the rule is available, its details are as follows: Rule group: MS-ThreatIntel-Response-CVEs Rule ID: 99006001 Default state: disabled. Customers need to enable the rule. Supported rulesets: DRS 2.0, 2.1 and 2.2. Unlike other WAF rules, this rule does not block or challenge any traffic. When the rule identifies malicious signals in the session that provides strong evidence of exploitation, it removes the potentially malicious elements from the response while leaving the remainder of the response unchanged. Mitigation for this rule takes effect only when the rule action is set to Block on anamoly. Please note that the response side mitigation does not generate WAF log entries or hit counts. Application Gateway WAF: rewrite rule Customers can apply an interim mitigation now using the HTTP header rewrite capability of Application Gateway, which is available on v2 SKU s . A WAF managed rule for Application Gateway is expected to roll out at a later date . Until then, we recommend the following rewrite rule: 1. Create a rewrite rule in a rewrite set associated with your routing rule(s). 2. Add a condition that evaluates the Set-Cookie response header against the following regular expression: ^PHPSESSID=(?:[a-zA-Z0-9\-]|%2[Cc])*(?:[^a-zA-Z0-9\-;%]|%(?!2[Cc]))+[a-zA-Z0-9\-]*[^;]+; 3. Set the action to delete the matching Set-Cookie response header. Alternatively, the header can be set to a replacement value of your choice. Please note that setting a value overwrites the entire header, including attributes such as Path=/; . Additional considerations: The rule applies only to a Set-Cookie header that matches the pattern. Other Set-Cookie headers in the same response are not affected. We recommend validating the rule on a non-production gateway before broader deployment. For further information, see Rewrite HTTP headers and URL with Azure Application Gateway . Application Gateway for Containers (AGC): A WAF managed rule for Application Gateway for Containers is expected to roll out at a later date . In the interim, customers can apply the custom rules. Application Gateway for Containers does not support regex-based rewrite rules on HTTP response. Restrict request size The proof-of-concept payloads analyzed so far are about 60 MB each. Attackers may be able to craft smaller payloads, so treat size limits as an extra layer of protection, not a mitigation on their own. Whatever rule set version you use, we recommend the following: Azure WAF on Application Gateway and Application Gateway for Containers The proof-of-concept payloads are well above the default maximum request body size of 128 KB on Application Gateway and Application Gateway for Containers. We recommend setting the maximum request body size in your WAF policy to the smallest value your application needs. Learn more . Azure WAF on Azure Front Door To limit request body size, create a custom rule with a size constraint. For request body checks, the size is measured on the decoded body. Set the limit to the smallest value your application needs and make sure request body inspection is enabled in your WAF policy settings. The following example blocks request bodies larger than 40 KB. items.summary_html:
Written in collaboration with yuvalpery​ and Gunjan Jain​  Introduction

Today, two critical remote code execution (RCE) vulnerabilities were disclosed in PHP. We strongly recommend that customers upgrade to a patched version of PHP as soon as possible. Upgrading is the only way to fully remediate these vulnerabilities. Read more on the PHP official website.

Microsoft has been part of the coordinated industry response to these vulnerabilities, working alongside the PHP Foundation, Wiz, security researchers, and other industry partners to help protect customers. Azure Web Application Firewall (WAF) has developed mitigations against known exploitation patterns to provide an additional layer of protection while customers apply the PHP security updates. These protections are intended to complement patching and are not a replacement for it. 

About the vulnerabilities: 
  1. CVE-2026-109618 - RCE via OOM corruption
  2. CVE-2026-109619- RCE via stale global state  

Both vulnerabilities can be exploited over the network without privileges or user interaction, with a high potential impact on confidentiality, integrity, and availability. 

The vulnerabilities relate to PHP handling of memory when a request terminates abnormally, for example due to memory exhaustion or a fatal error. Under certain conditions, improper memory handling could allow an attacker to achieve remote code execution. 

Fixed versions: 8.5.12, 8.4.27, 8.3.36, 8.2.35. 

Refer to vendor guidancefor patching of different versions of PHP.

Recommended action: upgrade PHP 

We recommend that customers: 

  1. Upgrade all PHP deployments to a patched version, including virtual machines, containers, base images, and platform runtimes. We suggest prioritizing internet-facing workloads. 
  2. Rebuild and redeploy container images that include their own PHP runtime, since updating the host does not update PHP inside an image. 
  3. Migrate to a supported PHP branch if the branch currently in use no longer receives security fixes. 
  4. Treat the Azure WAF mitigations below as a temporary, supplementary measure. They address a specific technique and do not remediate the underlying vulnerabilities. 
Azure WAF protection

If you are unable to upgrade PHP to a patched version immediately, apply the following mitigations in the interim -

  • Azure Front Door WAF: Apply the mitigation using custom rules for request-side mitigation and enable the managed rule for response-side mitigation.
  • Application Gateway WAF: Apply the mitigation using custom rules for request-side mitigation and enable the rewrite rule for response-side mitigation.
  • Application Gateway for Container WAF: Apply the mitigation using custom rules for request-side mitigation.

See below sections for details.

Mitigation using custom rules

These custom rules can help reduce exposure to selected request patterns associated with exploitation techniques for these vulnerabilities. Depending on application traffic, the rules may result in false positives and affect legitimate requests. They are intended as temporary mitigations and do not replace the need to upgrade PHP.  Learn more: Azure WAF custom rules for PHP2Shell mitigation. 

Request-side signals alone may not be sufficient to reliably identify certain exploitation attempts. Signals in the server response can provide additional evidence that malicious activity has occurred, enabling more targeted mitigation with higher confidence and lower false positives.  For this vulnerability, Azure WAF identifies known malicious patterns in the session and removes the potentially malicious elements from the response before it reaches the client. This provides an additional layer of protection for supported exploitation scenarios, while patching PHP remains necessary to fully address the underlying vulnerability.  

Azure Front Door WAF: managed rule 

A managed rule to handle potential attack vector in response is currently rolling out for Azure Front Door WAF, expected to complete October 28. Once the rule is available, its details are as follows: 

  • Rule group: MS-ThreatIntel-Response-CVEs 
  • Rule ID: 99006001 
  • Default state: disabled. Customers need to enable the rule. 

Supported rulesets: DRS 2.0, 2.1 and 2.2. Unlike other WAF rules, this rule does not block or challenge any traffic. When the rule identifies malicious signals in the session that provides strong evidence of exploitation, it removes the potentially malicious elements from the response while leaving the remainder of the response unchanged. Mitigation for this rule takes effect only when the rule action is set to Block on anamoly. Please note that the response side mitigation does not generate WAF log entries or hit counts.   

Application Gateway WAF: rewrite rule

Customers can apply an interim mitigation now using the HTTP header rewrite capability of Application Gateway, which is available on v2 SKUs. A WAF managed rule for Application Gateway is expected to roll out at a later date. Until then, we recommend the following rewrite rule: 

       1. Create a rewrite rule in a rewrite set associated with your routing rule(s). 

       2. Add a condition that evaluates the Set-Cookie response header against the following regular expression: 

^PHPSESSID=(?:[a-zA-Z0-9\-]|%2[Cc])*(?:[^a-zA-Z0-9\-;%]|%(?!2[Cc]))+[a-zA-Z0-9\-]*[^;]+; 

  

          3. Set the action to delete the matching Set-Cookie response header. Alternatively, the header can be set to a replacement value of your choice.                     Please note that setting a value overwrites the entire header, including attributes such as Path=/;. 

 

 Additional considerations: 

  • The rule applies only to a Set-Cookie header that matches the pattern. Other Set-Cookie headers in the same response are not affected. 
  • We recommend validating the rule on a non-production gateway before broader deployment. 

For further information, see Rewrite HTTP headers and URL with Azure Application Gateway. 

Application Gateway for Containers (AGC): A WAF managed rule for Application Gateway for Containers is expected to roll out at a later date. In the interim, customers can apply the custom rules. Application Gateway for Containers does not support regex-based rewrite rules on HTTP response. Restrict request size 

The proof-of-concept payloads analyzed so far are about 60 MB each. Attackers may be able to craft smaller payloads, so treat size limits as an extra layer of protection, not a mitigation on their own. Whatever rule set version you use, we recommend the following: 

Azure WAF on Application Gateway and Application Gateway for Containers 

The proof-of-concept payloads are well above the default maximum request body size of 128 KB on Application Gateway and Application Gateway for Containers. We recommend setting the maximum request body size in your WAF policy to the smallest value your application needs. Learn more.  

Azure WAF on Azure Front Door 

To limit request body size, create a custom rule with a size constraint. For request body checks, the size is measured on the decoded body. Set the limit to the smallest value your application needs and make sure request body inspection is enabled in your WAF policy settings. 

The following example blocks request bodies larger than 40 KB. This rule supports limits of up to 128 KB. 

 

{ "name": "BlockLargeRequestBody", "priority": 130, "enabledState": "Enabled", "ruleType": "MatchRule", "action": "Block", "matchConditions": [ { "matchVariable": "RequestBody", "operator": "GreaterThan", "negateCondition": false, "matchValue": [ "40960" ] } ] } Conclusion 

Following PHP security guidance and upgrading to a patched version is the recommended and complete remediation. Azure WAF mitigations can help reduce exposure during the upgrade period, and we encourage customers to upgrades at the earliest opportunity. 

Changelog
  • 10/26/2026 9:00 AM PST - Updated with additional guidance around request size restrictions
  • 10/21/2026 7:00 PM PST – Updated with additional guidance around custom rules

items.title: Protect against Brotli CVE-2026-111497 with Azure Web Application Firewall (WAF)
items.summary: Google Brotli versions 1.0.3 through 1.2.0 contain a buffer overflow vulnerability in the Brotli decoder, according to the recently published CVE-2026-111497 . A remote, unauthenticated attacker can send a crafted Brotli-compressed stream to corrupt decoder memory, expose sensitive memory contents, cause a denial of service, or potentially run arbitrary code. Any application that decompresses untrusted Brotli data may be affected. This includes Node.js and Python applications that bundle the vulnerable decoder, and services that accept request bodies with the Content-Encoding: br header. We strongly recommend upgrading Brotli to a patched version: 1.0.10, 1.1.1 or 1.2.1 ( Brotli releases ). If you use Node.js, upgrade to 22.23.4, 24.22.1 or 26.12.1 ( Node.js security release ). This rule may also block legitimate clients sending Brotli-compressed request bodies. If you aren't sure whether your application accepts them, set the action to 'Log traffic only' first, and review your WAF logs before switching to 'Deny traffic'. items.title: Microsoft Investigation Teams Issue Affecting Users in the United States
items.summary: Microsoft has restored Microsoft Teams service after investigating an issue affecting some users in the United States on October 26, 2026. The company tracked the disruption under incident TM1526111 and said automatic scaling efforts had returned the service to healthy levels. The recovery update changes the picture from Microsoft’s initial notice, which described a potential issue and confirmed that an investigation was underway. Microsoft has not identified the number of affected users or named the Teams features involved. Microsoft first alerted customers through its Microsoft 365 Status account , directing administrators to the Microsoft 365 admin center for incident details. Its initial statement limited the reported impact to some users in the United States, rather than describing a global outage. In a follow-up update , Microsoft said automated recovery actions were taking effect and that engineers were beginning to observe restoration. The company continued monitoring recovery while investigating what caused the disruption. Its latest status update said telemetry, the data used to track service performance, confirmed that automatic scaling had successfully increased processing throughput. In simple terms, the recovery process increased the service’s ability to handle work. Microsoft said service health had returned to normal, but the update did not explain the original trigger. The public statements do not establish a cyberattack, data breach, or account compromise. They also do not specify whether users experienced failed calls, delayed messages, meeting problems, or sign-in errors. Those details should not be inferred from the general incident notice. The incident follows Teams disruptions covered by Cybersecuritynews.com, including a September calling issue and an August outage affecting multiple features . These reports provide background on service availability, not evidence that the incidents share a cause. Administrators can check Health, then Service health, in the Microsoft 365 admin center and look for TM1526111. Microsoft’s service health guidance explains how this dashboard presents active incidents, investigation updates, and resolution notices. For organizations reviewing the disruption, the key distinction is between restored availability and a confirmed root cause. Microsoft’s latest update confirms recovery, while its public statements leave the initial cause unexplained. The incident record remains the reference for details. items.title: Hackers Can Hijack OpenAI Codex and Claude Code Using Malicious Files in Downloads Folder
items.summary: A plain text file placed in the Downloads folder can trick AI coding agents into changing their settings, installing malware, or exposing login tokens. Forever Security discovered the risk after stopping an agent on a real customer’s computer from installing a known malicious npm package. The company later reproduced separate attack paths against OpenAI Codex and Anthropic Claude Code in controlled tests. The incident began when Forever Security blocked an AI coding agent from installing a package named function-color . Investigators traced the order back to an AGENTS.md file stored in the customer’s ~/Downloads folder. The file looked like a normal set of engineering notes, but it contained carefully written instructions telling the agent to change its own setup and install the package. The source of the file remains unknown. Researchers did not prove that a malicious website placed it on the customer’s machine. Instead, they later showed that a website could deliver a file with the same name through normal browser download behavior, creating a possible path for the attack. An AGENTS.md file is similar to a README written for AI tools. OpenAI’s documentation says Codex reads these files before starting work and uses them to learn project rules, commands, and other instructions. Claude Code uses CLAUDE.md for a similar purpose and reads it at the start of a conversation. The danger comes from combining trusted agent instructions with a folder where web downloads normally arrive. A Markdown file cannot run by itself, so operating system checks designed for downloaded programs may not treat it as dangerous. The risk appears when an AI agent reads the text as trusted instructions and uses its own tools to carry them out. The attack is not fully automatic. The victim must run the coding agent from Downloads or otherwise allow it to process the planted instruction file. The agent must also have enough access to edit files, run commands, connect to the internet, or install packages. Approval prompts and sandbox controls can therefore reduce the chance of success. Codex Attack Creates Persistence In Forever Security’s controlled tests , Codex followed the malicious file in more than 90% of attempts. The instructions persuaded Codex to add an MCP server entry to ~/.codex/config.toml , its machine-wide configuration file, and start a second Codex session with approval and sandbox checks disabled. This change made the attack persistent. Once the rogue server was written into the global configuration, later Codex sessions could load it even when the user moved to another folder or project. Most tests used a harmless program, while the real malicious package was run once inside an isolated virtual machine. The package belonged to MALFEX, a long-running npm malware campaign targeting Windows developers. Checkmarx found that function-color pulled in function-flag , which could download and quietly run a Windows program. The wider campaign also used packages able to deliver remote-access malware and steal browser, Discord, Telegram, and cryptocurrency wallet data. More technical details are available in Cyber Security News’ report on the MALFEX npm malware campaign . Claude Code Exposed Tokens Claude Code required a different method. Researchers created a malicious CLAUDE.md that asked Claude to write an ANTHROPIC_BASE_URL value into .claude/settings.json . This redirected Claude’s API traffic to a server controlled by the researchers and exposed the OAuth token carried with the requests. Forever reported that Claude made the change in about half of its tests. The team replayed a captured token against Anthropic’s service and gained access as the victim. In some tests, the fake server also returned tool commands that led to code execution. Same-session execution through a helper agent worked about one-fifth of the time. The research adds to growing evidence that instruction files and add-ons can become a software supply-chain risk. Earlier research found that malicious agent skills targeting Claude Code and Codex could hide harmful actions from automated scanners. Developers should never start Codex, Claude Code, or another coding agent inside Downloads. Unknown AGENTS.md and CLAUDE.md files should be reviewed before an agent opens the folder. Users should also keep approval checks and sandboxes enabled, limit agent network access, and avoid instructions that request unsafe bypass options. Security teams should inspect ~/.codex/config.toml for unknown MCP servers and review .claude/settings.json for an unfamiliar ANTHROPIC_BASE_URL or proxy. Finding function-color , unexpected agent settings, or redirected API traffic should be treated as a possible compromise. Affected tokens and connected credentials should be revoked from a clean device, while the system should be isolated and checked for malware. Update defenses against new malware as soon as it appears. Integrate TI Feeds with data from 16K SOCs .

items.title: How to Export Google Cloud Audit Logs
items.summary: Use gcloud logging read with a filter on cloudaudit.googleapis.com, or run the same query in Logs Explorer and download the results as JSON: gcloud logging read 'logName:"cloudaudit.googleapis.com" AND timestamp>="2026-10-19T00:00:00Z" AND timestamp<"2026-10-20T00:00:00Z"' \ --project=my-project --format=json > gcp_audit_1019.json Admin Activity audit logs are always on and kept for 400 days. Data Access logs are off by default, except for BigQuery, and kept for 30 days once enabled. Cloud Audit Logs record who changed what in your Google Cloud projects: IAM grants, new service account keys, firewall changes, VMs spun up in odd regions. items.title: How to Export Okta System Logs
items.summary: In the Okta Admin Console, Reports → System Log lets you search events and download the results. For JSON, use the System Log API: GET /api/v1/logs with since and until, following the next link until it runs out. A short script is below. Okta keeps System Log events for 90 days. When identity is the perimeter, Okta’s System Log is the gate log. It records every sign-in, every MFA push, every factor reset and every admin role change. Prime Core has 58 detection rules for Okta data, mapped to 32 MITRE ATT&CK techniques. Among them: password spraying (T1110.003), MFA fatigue (T1621) and attackers tampering with MFA enrollment (T1556.006). Get Started for Free Before you start Retention is 90 days. Anything older exists only where you’ve been streaming or forwarding Okta logs, such as a SIEM. You need a token. An API token ( Security → API → Tokens ) inherits the permissions of the admin who created it. A read-only admin is enough for logs. For anything automated, an OAuth service app with the okta.logs.read scope is the cleaner choice. Either way, the token is a credential. Keep it out of shell history and revoke it when you’re done. Rate limits apply. The logs endpoint has its own rate limit. Big windows are fine, just not instant. Export with the System Log API This Python script pages through a time window and writes one event per line. It needs requests (pip install requests): import json, os, requests org = "https://yourorg.okta.com" headers = {"Authorization": f"SSWS {os.environ['OKTA_TOKEN']}", "Accept": "application/json"} url = f"{org}/api/v1/logs" params = {"since": "2026-10-19T00:00:00Z", "until": "2026-10-20T00:00:00Z", "limit": 1000} with open("okta_1019.jsonl", "w") as out: while url: r = requests.get(url, headers=headers, params=params, timeout=60) r.raise_for_status() events = r.json() for e in events: out.write(json.dumps(e) + "\n") if not events: break url = r.links.get("next", {}).get("url") params = None # the next link already carries the query Always set until . Without it, Okta treats the request as a live poll and keeps handing back a next link. Your loop would run forever, waiting for new events. To narrow it down, add a filter to params, for example “filter”: ‘eventType eq “user.session.start”‘. Or use “q”: “jane” for a keyword search. What to look for eventType Why it matters user.session.start with outcome.result: FAILURE Failed sign-ins; many users from one IP range means spraying user.mfa.okta_verify.deny_push User rejected a push; a burst of these is MFA fatigue in progress user.mfa.factor.deactivate, user.mfa.factor.reset_all Factors removed, often right after a helpdesk social-engineering call user.account.privilege.grant Admin role granted policy.rule.update, policy.lifecycle.update Sign-on or MFA policy changed, possibly weakened system.api_token.create A new API token, a quiet way to keep access The fields that tell the story: actor.alternateId (who), client.ipAddress and client.geographicalContext (from where), outcome (what happened), and debugContext.debugData (the details). Upload, sanitize and review in LogTotal Upload. Open logtotal.com and drop in the .jsonl file. [PROOF: upload screen, size limit] Sanitize. [PROOF: what gets masked: usernames and emails, IPs, device and session IDs]. Look it over before you continue. Review. [PROOF: what the results screen shows] When it goes wrong Symptom Likely cause Fix 401 Wrong or revoked token, or a missing SSWS prefix Check the header format; create a new token 403 Token creator lacks rights to read logs Use a token from an admin with log access 429 Rate limit hit Wait for the time in X-Rate-Limit-Reset, then continue The script never finishes No until in the query Set until Nothing older than 90 days Okta retention Check your SIEM or log streaming destination FAQ Can’t I just use the Admin Console? For a quick look at a short window, yes. For anything you want to analyze or keep, the API gives you complete JSON with every field. Does this cover Auth0? No. This guide is about Okta Workforce Identity. Auth0 has its own log format and API.

items.title: Where to Find Nginx and Apache Access Logs
items.summary: On Debian and Ubuntu, Nginx logs to /var/log/nginx/access.log and error.log, and Apache to /var/log/apache2/access.log and error.log. On RHEL, Rocky and Alma, Apache uses /var/log/httpd/access_log and error_log, with underscores and no extension. In containers built from the official Nginx image, there are no log files at all: everything goes to stdout and stderr, so docker logs is your export. The web server log is often the first place an intrusion leaves a trace: the scanner sweeping for .env files, the exploit string, the POST to a file that shouldn’t exist. Prime Core has 812 detection rules for web server logs, mapped to 337 MITRE ATT&CK techniques. Among them: exploitation of public-facing apps (T1190), web shells (T1505.003) and vulnerability scanning (T1595.002). Get Started for Free Before you start Find the real paths. Virtual hosts often log somewhere custom. Ask the server itself: # Nginx: dump the full effective config and pick out the log directives sudo nginx -T 2>/dev/null | grep -E 'access_log|error_log' # Apache sudo apachectl -S sudo grep -Ri -E 'CustomLog|ErrorLog' /etc/apache2/ /etc/httpd/ 2>/dev/null On Debian-based Apache, virtual hosts without their own CustomLog end up in other_vhosts_access.log. People miss that one all the time. Check whose IP you’re logging. Behind a load balancer, CDN or reverse proxy, every request can appear to come from the proxy. That holds unless the server is set up to log the real client: set_real_ip_from and real_ip_header in Nginx, mod_remoteip in Apache. If every line shows the same few internal IPs, the attacker’s address is only in X-Forwarded-For, if you log it, or in the proxy’s own logs. Check the format. Both servers default to the “combined” format, but plenty of setups customize it (log_format in Nginx, LogFormat in Apache). Note what yours looks like before uploading. Permissions. On Debian and Ubuntu these logs are readable by root and the adm group; elsewhere, plan on sudo. Export from log files Logs rotate daily or weekly, so include the rotated files. zcat -f reads plain and gzipped files alike: # Nginx, current and rotated, oldest first sudo zcat -f $(ls -tr /var/log/nginx/access.log*) > web-03_nginx_access.log # Apache on RHEL sudo zcat -f $(ls -tr /var/log/httpd/access_log*) > web-03_httpd_access.lo For a single day, combined-format timestamps make grep enough: grep '19/Oct/2026' web-03_nginx_access.log > web-03_access_1019.log Take the error log as well. Upstream failures, PHP errors and some exploit attempts show up only there. Export from containers # Docker: stdout is the access log, stderr the error log docker logs --since 2026-10-19T00:00:00 --until 2026-10-20T00:00:00 nginx > nginx_access.log 2> nginx_error.log # Kubernetes kubectl logs deploy/nginx --since=24h > nginx.log Container logs disappear with the container unless something collects them. If the pod was replaced, check your cluster’s log collector instead. What to look for Pattern What it usually means Bursts of 404s for /.env, /.git/config, /wp-login.php, /phpmyadmin Automated scanning ../, ${jndi:, union select,

How to Export Kubernetes Audit Logs
items.summary: Where Kubernetes audit logs live depends on who runs your control plane. On a self-managed cluster, they’re a JSON-lines file on the control plane node, at whatever path –audit-log-path points to. On EKS, they go to CloudWatch Logs, on AKS to a Log Analytics workspace or storage account, and on GKE to Cloud Audit Logs. One thing holds everywhere: audit logging has to be switched on. On self-managed clusters and EKS it’s off until someone enables it. The audit log records every request to the Kubernetes API: who ran kubectl exec into which pod, who read which secret, who bound themselves to cluster-admin. Prime Core has 93 detection rules for Kubernetes audit data, mapped to 220 MITRE ATT&CK techniques. Among them: exec into running containers (T1609), deploying rogue containers (T1610) and reading credentials through the container API (T1552.007). Get Started for Free Before you start Is it enabled? Platform Where to check Self-managed (kubeadm and similar) –audit-policy-file and –audit-log-path on the API server; with kubeadm, in /etc/kubernetes/manifests/kube-apiserver.yaml EKS Cluster → Observability → control plane logging, “audit” log type AKS Diagnostic settings on the cluster, categories kube-audit or kube-audit-admin GKE On by default for Admin Activity; Data Access logging for Kubernetes is opt-in If it wasn’t on, there’s nothing to export for the past, and the rest of this guide is about next time. Detail depends on the policy. At Metadata level you see who did what to which object. At Request or RequestResponse level you also see the bodies, for example the pod spec that asked for privileged: true. Know which one you have before you go looking. Expect volume. Controllers and service accounts talk to the API constantly. On AKS, kube-audit-admin leaves out read-only get and list calls, which keeps size sane but also hides secret reads. Export it Self-managed cluster , on a control plane node: # confirm the path first sudo grep -- '--audit-log-path' /etc/kubernetes/manifests/kube-apiserver.yaml sudo cat /var/log/kubernetes/audit/audit.log > k8s_audit.jsonl Rotated files (from –audit-log-maxbackup) sit next to it with a timestamp in the name. Include them if the window reaches back. EKS , from CloudWatch Logs: aws logs filter-log-events --log-group-name /aws/eks/my-cluster/cluster \ --log-stream-name-prefix kube-apiserver-audit \ --start-time $(date -d '2026-10-19T00:00:00Z' +%s000) --end-time $(date -d '2026-10-20T00:00:00Z' +%s000) \ --output json | jq -c '.events[].message | fromjson' > eks_audit_1019.jsonl Each CloudWatch event wraps the audit entry as a string; fromjson unwraps it. The date -d syntax is GNU; on macOS, compute the millisecond timestamps another way. AKS , from Log Analytics (resource-specific tables): az monitor log-analytics query -w \ --analytics-query "AKSAuditAdmin | where TimeGenerated between (datetime(2026-10-19) .. datetime(2026-10-20))" \ --output json > aks_audit_1019.json GKE , from Cloud Audit Logs: gcloud logging read 'resource.type="k8s_cluster" AND logName:"cloudaudit.googleapis.com" AND timestamp>="2026-10-19T00:00:00Z" AND timestamp<"2026-10-20T00:00:00Z"' \ --project=my-project --format=json | jq -c '.[]' > gke_audit_1019.jsonl What to look for Request Why it matters create on pods/exec (objectRef.subresource: exec) Someone opened a shell inside a running container create of a ClusterRoleBinding to cluster-admin Privilege escalation to full control get or list on secrets by an unusual identity Credential harvesting Pods created with privileged, hostPath or hostNetwork A step toward escaping onto the node user.username: system:anonymous with a 2xx response Anonymous access that shouldn’t work Bursts of 403 from one service account A stolen token feeling out its permissions Upload, sanitize and review in LogTotal Upload. Open logtotal.com and drop in the .jsonl file. Sanitize. [what gets masked: usernames, service account names, source IPs, namespaces, object names]. Look it over before you continue. Review. When it goes wrong Symptom Likely cause Fix No audit file on the control plane API server has no audit policy configured Expected; configure it for the future EKS log group or audit streams missing The “audit” control plane log type isn’t enabled Enable it for the future Each line is one long escaped string CloudWatch wrapping Unwrap with fromjson, as above You can see who changed a pod, but not how Policy is at Metadata level Raise the level for sensitive resources No secret reads in AKS data kube-audit-admin excludes get and list Collect kube-audit if you need them FAQ Aren’t container logs enough? No. Container logs show what an application printed. The audit log shows what people and service accounts did to the cluster. Different questions, different logs. Can I read the audit file on a managed cluster? No. On EKS, AKS and GKE, you don’t get access to the control plane nodes. The provider’s logging service is the only route.

Detail depends on the policy. At Metadata level you see who did what to which object. At Request or RequestResponse level you also see the bodies, for example the pod spec that asked for privileged: true. Know which one you have before you go looking.

Expect volume. Controllers and service accounts talk to the API constantly. On AKS, kube-audit-admin leaves out read-only get and list calls, which keeps size sane but also hides secret reads.

Export it

Self-managed cluster, on a control plane node:

# confirm the path first

sudo grep -- '--audit-log-path' /etc/kubernetes/manifests/kube-apiserver.yaml


sudo cat /var/log/kubernetes/audit/audit.log > k8s_audit.jsonl

Rotated files (from –audit-log-maxbackup) sit next to it with a timestamp in the name. Include them if the window reaches back.

EKS, from CloudWatch Logs:

aws logs filter-log-events --log-group-name /aws/eks/my-cluster/cluster \

  --log-stream-name-prefix kube-apiserver-audit \

  --start-time $(date -d '2026-10-19T00:00:00Z' +%s000) --end-time $(date -d '2026-10-20T00:00:00Z' +%s000) \

  --output json | jq -c '.events[].message | fromjson' > eks_audit_1019.jsonl

Each CloudWatch event wraps the audit entry as a string; fromjson unwraps it. The date -d syntax is GNU; on macOS, compute the millisecond timestamps another way.

AKS, from Log Analytics (resource-specific tables):

az monitor log-analytics query -w  \

  --analytics-query "AKSAuditAdmin | where TimeGenerated between (datetime(2026-10-19) .. datetime(2026-10-20))" \

  --output json > aks_audit_1019.json

GKE, from Cloud Audit Logs:

gcloud logging read 'resource.type="k8s_cluster" AND logName:"cloudaudit.googleapis.com" AND timestamp>="2026-10-19T00:00:00Z" AND timestamp<"2026-10-20T00:00:00Z"' \

  --project=my-project --format=json | jq -c '.[]' > gke_audit_1019.jsonl
What to look for RequestWhy it matterscreate on pods/exec (objectRef.subresource: exec)Someone opened a shell inside a running containercreate of a ClusterRoleBinding to cluster-adminPrivilege escalation to full controlget or list on secrets by an unusual identityCredential harvestingPods created with privileged, hostPath or hostNetworkA step toward escaping onto the nodeuser.username: system:anonymous with a 2xx responseAnonymous access that shouldn’t workBursts of 403 from one service accountA stolen token feeling out its permissions Upload, sanitize and review in LogTotal
  1. Upload. Open logtotal.com and drop in the .jsonl file.
  2. Sanitize. [what gets masked: usernames, service account names, source IPs, namespaces, object names]. Look it over before you continue.
  3. Review.
When it goes wrong SymptomLikely causeFixNo audit file on the control planeAPI server has no audit policy configuredExpected; configure it for the futureEKS log group or audit streams missingThe “audit” control plane log type isn’t enabledEnable it for the futureEach line is one long escaped stringCloudWatch wrappingUnwrap with fromjson, as aboveYou can see who changed a pod, but not howPolicy is at Metadata levelRaise the level for sensitive resourcesNo secret reads in AKS datakube-audit-admin excludes get and listCollect kube-audit if you need them
FAQ

Aren’t container logs enough?

No. Container logs show what an application printed. The audit log shows what people and service accounts did to the cluster. Different questions, different logs.

Can I read the audit file on a managed cluster?

No. On EKS, AKS and GKE, you don’t get access to the control plane nodes. The provider’s logging service is the only route.
