items.title: CVE-2026-115560: New Unpatched PHP RCE Risk Requires Immediate Mitigation
items.summary: PHP has disclosed CVE-2026-115560, a new remote code execution risk affecting web applications that use an unusual combination of PHP session configuration and runtime behavior. The issue was disclosed on October 23, 2026, only two days after PHP released emergency fixes for the critical PHP2Shell vulnerabilities CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619. Unlike those earlier vulnerabilities, CVE-2026-115560 has not triggered another emergency PHP release. The PHP security team considers the vulnerable configuration unlikely in typical deployments and plans to address the flaw through its next regular bugfix cycle. Until then, administrators are advised to disable PHP’s session upload progress feature where the vulnerable configuration may exist. The new vulnerability is also important because installing PHP 8.5.12, 8.4.27, 8.3.36, or 8.2.35—the releases that fixed the two earlier PHP2Shell flaws—does not remediate CVE-2026-115560. Fully updated systems may therefore remain exposed if their applications meet the specific configuration prerequisites. Security teams seeking CVE-2026-115560 detection opportunities should prioritize visibility into PHP session handling, unusual multipart uploads, unexpected changes to session serialization behavior, and suspicious child processes spawned by PHP or web-server workers. SOC Prime’s AI-Native Detection Intelligence Platform enables security teams to strengthen coverage for emerging vulnerability exploitation and related post-compromise behavior across SIEM, EDR, and Data Lake environments. Click Explore Detections to access relevant detection content and hunting logic. To Detect CVE-2026-115560, defenders should combine PHP configuration assessment with web, endpoint, application, and reverse-proxy telemetry while a vendor patch remains unavailable. Security practitioners can also leverage Prime Architect to transform newly disclosed vulnerability intelligence into Sigma rules and hunting queries, validate detection logic, and translate relevant detections across supported security platforms. Contact Sales CVE-2026-115560 analysis PHP published an informational advisory on October 23 describing a potentially exploitable interaction between session serialization and the session upload progress feature. According to the PHP security team, an application must satisfy several specific conditions before the issue can occur: session.serialize_handler must initially be configured as php_binary or php_serialize. Application code must subsequently change the handler to php at runtime using ini_set(). That change must occur before session_start() is called. session.upload_progress.enabled must remain enabled. Applications that never switch the serialization handler at runtime are not exposed through this specific path and can continue using session upload progress. PHP describes the vulnerable combination as uncommon. This distinction substantially narrows the attack surface compared with CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619. The earlier PHP2Shell vulnerabilities affected web-serving PHP installations broadly and required emergency updates. CVE-2026-115560 instead depends on application-specific configuration and code behavior. The details for CVE-2026-115560 remain intentionally limited. PHP has not yet published the complete technical root cause, exact vulnerable version ranges, a CVSS score, or the specific internal memory or session state transition that ultimately produces the RCE condition. The vendor says those details will be included with the next regular release. Based on the disclosed prerequisites, the vulnerability appears connected to inconsistent handling of session data when an application changes serialization formats during request processing while PHP’s upload-progress mechanism is active. However, the exact exploitation primitive should not be inferred beyond what PHP has formally disclosed. CVE-2026-115560 affects applications meeting the vulnerable configuration pattern, including applications running fully patched PHP releases containing the October 21 PHP2Shell fixes. PHP has not yet stated which PHP branches or historical releases contain the underlying flaw. This means administrators should not determine exposure solely from the installed PHP version. Instead, they need to assess application and server configuration. A useful first step is checking whether session upload progress is enabled: session.upload_progress.enabled=1 Administrators should also identify any application code calling ini_set() to modify session.serialize_handler, particularly transitions from php_binary or php_serialize to php. The new flaw is separate from CVE-2026-109619 even though the mitigation overlaps. Disabling session upload progress was already recommended as a risk-reduction measure for one of the original PHP2Shell vulnerabilities. Organizations that kept that setting disabled after the October 21 emergency update are already protected against the newly disclosed path, according to PHP. There is currently no public CVE-2026-115560 PoC documented by PHP or the two supplied reports. The security team has also not disclosed enough technical information to reproduce the vulnerability reliably from the public advisory alone. This is notably different from the earlier PHP2Shell flaws, for which various proof-of-concept attempts and exploit activity emerged around disclosure. Those attacks should not be attributed to the new vulnerability. No exploitation of CVE-2026-115560 has been reported as of October 26, 2026. The Hacker News specifically distinguishes ongoing PHP2Shell scanning and exploitation attempts from this newer vulnerability, noting that the observed activity targets CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619. As a result, CVE-2026-115560 IOCs such as malicious IP addresses, domains, hashes, payloads, or confirmed exploit request patterns are not currently available. Until more technical details emerge, defenders should focus on behavioral and configuration-based indicators, including: PHP applications changing session.serialize_handler during execution Session upload progress remaining enabled on applications with custom session logic Unexpected multipart POST traffic to applications handling PHP sessions PHP-FPM, php-cgi, Apache, or other PHP-serving processes spawning shells or scripting interpreters Unexpected outbound network connections from PHP workers Newly created files inside web roots or writable application directories Unusual changes to session files or session storage Web shells, scheduled jobs, or unauthorized persistence created by PHP service accounts Application developers should also review custom session-handling logic. Framework extensions, legacy applications, internal platforms, or custom authentication systems are more likely than straightforward PHP deployments to modify serialization settings dynamically. The disclosure comes during an already active period of PHP exploitation activity. The original PHP2Shell vulnerabilities were patched on October 21, and multiple security companies subsequently observed widespread probing and exploit attempts. However, PHP and security researchers have not linked those campaigns to CVE-2026-115560. CVE-2026-115560 mitigation PHP currently recommends one direct defensive measure: session.upload_progress.enabled=0 Administrators should apply the setting through php.ini, PHP-FPM pool configuration, Apache configuration, or another server-level mechanism that takes effect before request processing. Organizations that disabled the feature while mitigating CVE-2026-109619 and have left it disabled do not need an additional configuration change for this vulnerability. After changing the setting, restart PHP workers and relevant web services to ensure existing processes load the updated configuration. Depending on the environment, this may include restarting PHP-FPM pools, Apache workers, containers, or other PHP application runtime processes. Administrators can verify the effective setting through PHP configuration inspection rather than assuming a central php.ini value applies everywhere. PHP deployments frequently combine settings from: Global php.ini conf.d files PHP-FPM pool configuration Apache directives Container-specific configuration Application-level .user.ini Runtime calls to ini_set() The most important exposure assessment is application-specific. Search application source code for runtime modification of the session serializer, particularly patterns involving: ini_set(‘session.serialize_handler’, ‘php’) Applications that never change the serializer from php_binary or php_serialize to php before session_start() do not match the vulnerable scenario PHP has disclosed. Organizations should nevertheless maintain the October 21 PHP2Shell security updates. Disabling upload progress addresses the newly identified path but does not replace the emergency fixes for CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619. Supported installations should therefore remain on at least: PHP 8.5.12 PHP 8.4.27 PHP 8.3.36 PHP 8.2.35 Those releases remediate the earlier PHP2Shell issues but not the newly disclosed vulnerability. Security teams should also inventory unsupported PHP installations. PHP 8.1 and earlier releases no longer receive routine upstream security updates, meaning organizations operating legacy environments may have difficulty determining complete exposure once the final CVE advisory is published. If disabling session upload progress is operationally impossible, organizations should first determine whether their applications actually modify the serialization handler dynamically. PHP explicitly states that applications that never perform this runtime switch can leave session upload progress enabled. As additional safeguards, defenders can: Limit external access to sensitive PHP applications. Apply restrictive reverse-proxy rules around unnecessary file-upload endpoints. Monitor multipart requests associated with PHP sessions. Alert on anomalous PHP worker child processes. Apply least privilege to PHP-FPM and web-server accounts. Prevent PHP services from writing to executable directories where possible. Restrict outbound connectivity from web application workloads. Monitor web roots and temporary directories for unauthorized file creation. AWS has also noted that its PHP application WAF rules can block POST requests combining PHP session identifiers with the PHP_SESSION_UPLOAD_PROGRESS field, providing another defensive layer for environments that cannot immediately make configuration changes. This type of filtering should still be considered defense in depth rather than a replacement for PHP’s recommended configuration change. Once PHP releases the regular bugfix update containing the permanent fix, organizations should deploy it promptly even if the temporary mitigation is already enabled. After patching, administrators can decide whether session upload progress needs to be re-enabled based on application requirements. If exploitation is suspected, isolate the affected application server and preserve web, PHP, reverse-proxy, endpoint, and network telemetry. Review writable directories for web shells or newly created files, inspect PHP child processes, and identify credentials or secrets accessible to the compromised service. Because successful exploitation could potentially result in code execution with the privileges of the PHP worker, responders should rotate relevant application credentials, database secrets, API tokens, cloud keys, and other sensitive information if compromise cannot be excluded. Disclaimer: Detection content may not be available for every CVE. Check the SOC Prime Platform for current coverage. If relevant detections are not yet available, check again as new threat intelligence and detection content are continuously added. FAQ What is CVE-2026-115560 and how does it work? CVE-2026-115560 is an unpatched PHP remote code execution vulnerability involving an unusual interaction between session serialization and PHP’s session upload progress feature. The vulnerable scenario requires an application to configure session.serialize_handler as php_binary or php_serialize, change it to php at runtime using ini_set(), and do so before session_start() while session upload progress remains enabled. PHP has not yet disclosed the complete exploitation mechanism and plans to publish a full advisory with its next regular bugfix release. When was CVE-2026-115560 first discovered? PHP publicly disclosed the issue on October 23, 2026 through an informational advisory, two days after releasing emergency fixes for CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619. The vendor has not published the exact date when the flaw was originally discovered or identified internally. What is the impact of CVE-2026-115560 on systems? Successful exploitation could allow an attacker to execute code within the context of a vulnerable PHP web application. The potential downstream impact depends on the privileges assigned to the PHP service and may include access to application data, credential theft, malicious file creation, persistence, and interaction with backend databases or cloud services. However, PHP considers the required configuration uncommon and has not yet published a severity score or evidence of real-world exploitation. Can CVE-2026-115560 still affect me in 2026? Yes. As of October 26, 2026, no permanent security patch has been released. Importantly, the PHP 8.5.12, 8.4.27, 8.3.36, and 8.2.35 releases issued on October 21 do not fix this vulnerability. Applications using those fully patched versions can still be exposed if they meet the configuration prerequisites. PHP plans to include the fix in its next regular bugfix release. How can I protect myself from CVE-2026-115560? Set session.upload_progress.enabled=0 and restart all PHP workers and relevant web services. Review application code for runtime changes to session.serialize_handler, particularly transitions from php_binary or php_serialize to php before session_start(). Continue running the latest PHP security release to remain protected from CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619, and deploy the forthcoming PHP release containing the permanent fix for this vulnerability as soon as it becomes available.
items.summary_html:
PHP has disclosed CVE-2026-115560, a new remote code execution risk affecting web applications that use an unusual combination of PHP session configuration and runtime behavior. The issue was disclosed on October 23, 2026, only two days after PHP released emergency fixes for the critical PHP2Shell vulnerabilities CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619.

Unlike those earlier vulnerabilities, CVE-2026-115560 has not triggered another emergency PHP release. The PHP security team considers the vulnerable configuration unlikely in typical deployments and plans to address the flaw through its next regular bugfix cycle. Until then, administrators are advised to disable PHP’s session upload progress feature where the vulnerable configuration may exist.

The new vulnerability is also important because installing PHP 8.5.12, 8.4.27, 8.3.36, or 8.2.35—the releases that fixed the two earlier PHP2Shell flaws—does not remediate CVE-2026-115560. Fully updated systems may therefore remain exposed if their applications meet the specific configuration prerequisites.

Security teams seeking CVE-2026-115560 detection opportunities should prioritize visibility into PHP session handling, unusual multipart uploads, unexpected changes to session serialization behavior, and suspicious child processes spawned by PHP or web-server workers.

SOC Prime’s AI-Native Detection Intelligence Platform enables security teams to strengthen coverage for emerging vulnerability exploitation and related post-compromise behavior across SIEM, EDR, and Data Lake environments.

Click Explore Detections to access relevant detection content and hunting logic. To Detect CVE-2026-115560, defenders should combine PHP configuration assessment with web, endpoint, application, and reverse-proxy telemetry while a vendor patch remains unavailable.

Security practitioners can also leverage Prime Architect to transform newly disclosed vulnerability intelligence into Sigma rules and hunting queries, validate detection logic, and translate relevant detections across supported security platforms.

Contact Sales

CVE-2026-115560 analysis

PHP published an informational advisory on October 23 describing a potentially exploitable interaction between session serialization and the session upload progress feature.

According to the PHP security team, an application must satisfy several specific conditions before the issue can occur:

  • session.serialize_handler must initially be configured as php_binary or php_serialize.
  • Application code must subsequently change the handler to php at runtime using ini_set().
  • That change must occur before session_start() is called.
  • session.upload_progress.enabled must remain enabled.

Applications that never switch the serialization handler at runtime are not exposed through this specific path and can continue using session upload progress. PHP describes the vulnerable combination as uncommon.

This distinction substantially narrows the attack surface compared with CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619. The earlier PHP2Shell vulnerabilities affected web-serving PHP installations broadly and required emergency updates. CVE-2026-115560 instead depends on application-specific configuration and code behavior.

The details for CVE-2026-115560 remain intentionally limited. PHP has not yet published the complete technical root cause, exact vulnerable version ranges, a CVSS score, or the specific internal memory or session state transition that ultimately produces the RCE condition. The vendor says those details will be included with the next regular release.

Based on the disclosed prerequisites, the vulnerability appears connected to inconsistent handling of session data when an application changes serialization formats during request processing while PHP’s upload-progress mechanism is active. However, the exact exploitation primitive should not be inferred beyond what PHP has formally disclosed.

CVE-2026-115560 affects applications meeting the vulnerable configuration pattern, including applications running fully patched PHP releases containing the October 21 PHP2Shell fixes. PHP has not yet stated which PHP branches or historical releases contain the underlying flaw.

This means administrators should not determine exposure solely from the installed PHP version. Instead, they need to assess application and server configuration.

A useful first step is checking whether session upload progress is enabled:

session.upload_progress.enabled=1

Administrators should also identify any application code calling ini_set() to modify session.serialize_handler, particularly transitions from php_binary or php_serialize to php.

The new flaw is separate from CVE-2026-109619 even though the mitigation overlaps. Disabling session upload progress was already recommended as a risk-reduction measure for one of the original PHP2Shell vulnerabilities. Organizations that kept that setting disabled after the October 21 emergency update are already protected against the newly disclosed path, according to PHP.

There is currently no public CVE-2026-115560 PoC documented by PHP or the two supplied reports. The security team has also not disclosed enough technical information to reproduce the vulnerability reliably from the public advisory alone.

This is notably different from the earlier PHP2Shell flaws, for which various proof-of-concept attempts and exploit activity emerged around disclosure. Those attacks should not be attributed to the new vulnerability.

No exploitation of CVE-2026-115560 has been reported as of October 26, 2026. The Hacker News specifically distinguishes ongoing PHP2Shell scanning and exploitation attempts from this newer vulnerability, noting that the observed activity targets CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619.

As a result, CVE-2026-115560 IOCs such as malicious IP addresses, domains, hashes, payloads, or confirmed exploit request patterns are not currently available.

Until more technical details emerge, defenders should focus on behavioral and configuration-based indicators, including:

  • PHP applications changing session.serialize_handler during execution
  • Session upload progress remaining enabled on applications with custom session logic
  • Unexpected multipart POST traffic to applications handling PHP sessions
  • PHP-FPM, php-cgi, Apache, or other PHP-serving processes spawning shells or scripting interpreters
  • Unexpected outbound network connections from PHP workers
  • Newly created files inside web roots or writable application directories
  • Unusual changes to session files or session storage
  • Web shells, scheduled jobs, or unauthorized persistence created by PHP service accounts

Application developers should also review custom session-handling logic. Framework extensions, legacy applications, internal platforms, or custom authentication systems are more likely than straightforward PHP deployments to modify serialization settings dynamically.

The disclosure comes during an already active period of PHP exploitation activity. The original PHP2Shell vulnerabilities were patched on October 21, and multiple security companies subsequently observed widespread probing and exploit attempts. However, PHP and security researchers have not linked those campaigns to CVE-2026-115560.

CVE-2026-115560 mitigation

PHP currently recommends one direct defensive measure:

session.upload_progress.enabled=0

Administrators should apply the setting through php.ini, PHP-FPM pool configuration, Apache configuration, or another server-level mechanism that takes effect before request processing.

Organizations that disabled the feature while mitigating CVE-2026-109619 and have left it disabled do not need an additional configuration change for this vulnerability.

After changing the setting, restart PHP workers and relevant web services to ensure existing processes load the updated configuration. Depending on the environment, this may include restarting PHP-FPM pools, Apache workers, containers, or other PHP application runtime processes.

Administrators can verify the effective setting through PHP configuration inspection rather than assuming a central php.ini value applies everywhere. PHP deployments frequently combine settings from:

  • Global php.ini
  • conf.d files
  • PHP-FPM pool configuration
  • Apache directives
  • Container-specific configuration
  • Application-level .user.ini
  • Runtime calls to ini_set()

The most important exposure assessment is application-specific. Search application source code for runtime modification of the session serializer, particularly patterns involving:

ini_set(‘session.serialize_handler’, ‘php’)

Applications that never change the serializer from php_binary or php_serialize to php before session_start() do not match the vulnerable scenario PHP has disclosed.

Organizations should nevertheless maintain the October 21 PHP2Shell security updates. Disabling upload progress addresses the newly identified path but does not replace the emergency fixes for CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619.

Supported installations should therefore remain on at least:

  • PHP 8.5.12
  • PHP 8.4.27
  • PHP 8.3.36
  • PHP 8.2.35

Those releases remediate the earlier PHP2Shell issues but not the newly disclosed vulnerability.

Security teams should also inventory unsupported PHP installations. PHP 8.1 and earlier releases no longer receive routine upstream security updates, meaning organizations operating legacy environments may have difficulty determining complete exposure once the final CVE advisory is published.

If disabling session upload progress is operationally impossible, organizations should first determine whether their applications actually modify the serialization handler dynamically. PHP explicitly states that applications that never perform this runtime switch can leave session upload progress enabled.

As additional safeguards, defenders can:

  • Limit external access to sensitive PHP applications.
  • Apply restrictive reverse-proxy rules around unnecessary file-upload endpoints.
  • Monitor multipart requests associated with PHP sessions.
  • Alert on anomalous PHP worker child processes.
  • Apply least privilege to PHP-FPM and web-server accounts.
  • Prevent PHP services from writing to executable directories where possible.
  • Restrict outbound connectivity from web application workloads.
  • Monitor web roots and temporary directories for unauthorized file creation.

AWS has also noted that its PHP application WAF rules can block POST requests combining PHP session identifiers with the PHP_SESSION_UPLOAD_PROGRESS field, providing another defensive layer for environments that cannot immediately make configuration changes. This type of filtering should still be considered defense in depth rather than a replacement for PHP’s recommended configuration change.

Once PHP releases the regular bugfix update containing the permanent fix, organizations should deploy it promptly even if the temporary mitigation is already enabled.

After patching, administrators can decide whether session upload progress needs to be re-enabled based on application requirements.

If exploitation is suspected, isolate the affected application server and preserve web, PHP, reverse-proxy, endpoint, and network telemetry. Review writable directories for web shells or newly created files, inspect PHP child processes, and identify credentials or secrets accessible to the compromised service.

Because successful exploitation could potentially result in code execution with the privileges of the PHP worker, responders should rotate relevant application credentials, database secrets, API tokens, cloud keys, and other sensitive information if compromise cannot be excluded.

What is the impact of CVE-2026-115560 on systems?

Successful exploitation could allow an attacker to execute code within the context of a vulnerable PHP web application. The potential downstream impact depends on the privileges assigned to the PHP service and may include access to application data, credential theft, malicious file creation, persistence, and interaction with backend databases or cloud services. However, PHP considers the required configuration uncommon and has not yet published a severity score or evidence of real-world exploitation.

Can CVE-2026-115560 still affect me in 2026?

Yes. As of October 26, 2026, no permanent security patch has been released. Importantly, the PHP 8.5.12, 8.4.27, 8.3.36, and 8.2.35 releases issued on October 21 do not fix this vulnerability. Applications using those fully patched versions can still be exposed if they meet the configuration prerequisites. PHP plans to include the fix in its next regular bugfix release.

Proofpoint’s Core Email Protection API solution joins the Microsoft Defender ICES vendor ecosystem
items.summary: Email remains the most exploited gateway for cyberattacks, as the threat landscape continues to get more sophisticated with attackers using AI to scale phishing, malware, and business email compromise. Microsoft Defender is a leading email security solution , helping organizations stay ahead of these threats with a modern, cloud-native approach. At the same time, many organizations choose to layer additional email security solutions to meet compliance requirements or align to an existing defense-in-depth strategy. This approach can strengthen resilience, but it can also add operational complexity for SOC teams. That’s why one year ago, we introduced the Microsoft Defender Integrated Cloud Email Security (ICES) vendor ecosystem , which is designed to simplify that complexity by integrating partner protections into Microsoft Defender. Today, we’re continuing to expand the ICES vendor ecosystem by adding Proofpoint Core Email Protection API . Proofpoint joins existing members Darktrace, KnowBe4, Cisco, and VIPRE Security Group. How joint customers benefit from a streamlined SOC experience in Microsoft Defender The ICES ecosystem brings trusted third-party email security verdicts and telemetry into the Defender portal through an API-based integration model. This allows Microsoft Defender to acknowledge partner verdicts on messages, apply the highest-severity determination, and surface that information in the same investigation and response workflows security teams already use. The integration with Proofpoint Core Email Protection API is designed specifically for customers who have already chosen to deploy Proofpoint’s ICES solution alongside Microsoft Defender. It supports environments where customers run both solutions and want to reduce friction for their SOC teams. By integrating Proofpoint into the ICES ecosystem, customers can now preserve their existing security strategy while improving how investigations and response are carried out day to day. "Organizations rely on both Microsoft and Proofpoint to protect their most critical communications and data. By extending Proofpoint’s interoperability across ICES, we’re delivering a more unified security experience that strengthens defense-in-depth and simplifies operations for our shared customers. This milestone reflects our commitment to joint customers worldwide.” - Tom Corn, EVP and GM, Threat Protection Group at Proofpoint Below we have outlined how Proofpoint’s ICES solution now integrates within Microsoft Defender: Unified quarantine: Quarantine is the central place where suspicious, unwanted, or malicious messages are held so they do not remain in users’ mailboxes while analysts review them. With unified quarantine, teams can view and manage quarantined email from both Defender and supported ICES vendors in one experience. The benefit is less context switching, faster triage, and a more consistent response workflow because analysts do not need to jump between separate admin consoles to understand what was held and why. In Figure 1, you can see that in the column “detection technology” ThirdPartyFiltering is listed, indicating to you that this was directly contributed by Proofpoint’s Core Email Protection API solution. Figure 1: Emails quarantined by Proofpoint Core Email Protection API show up in the quarantine experience in Defender, alongside Defender-quarantined emails. Streamlined operations: ICES integrations make Defender more actionable for SOC teams by extending familiar investigation experiences across Microsoft and partner-detected email. In Threat Explorer, analysts can review messages actioned by Defender and integrated partners in one place, making it easier to correlate verdicts and understand which layer acted on a message. Figure 2 and 3 : Shows how you can review emails actioned by Proofpoint by using ‘ThirdPartyFiltering’ in Threat Explorer. Click on a particular row and dive deeper into delivery and email details. In Advanced Hunting , teams can query email events that include third-party detections to investigate patterns, validate coverage, and hunt for missed or emerging threats. And on the Email entity page, analysts can see message-level details and action history, including which product took action and what verdict was assigned. Together, these experiences give teams a more complete investigation workflow without forcing them to jump between separate consoles. Figure 4: Shows the Advanced Hunting page in the Defender portal where analysts can query email events, including third-party detections. Reinforcing Our Commitment to Customer Choice The continued expansion of the ICES vendor ecosystem reinforces Microsoft’s commitment to supporting customers who strategically layer email security solutions. The goal of our ecosystem is making multiple solutions operationally effective together with Microsoft Defender as the shared Security Operations experience. Email remains the most exploited gateway for cyberattacks, as the threat landscape continues to get more sophisticated with attackers using AI to scale phishing, malware, and business email compromise. Microsoft Defender is a leading email security solution, helping organizations stay ahead of these threats with a modern, cloud-native approach. At the same time, many organizations choose to layer additional email security solutions to meet compliance requirements or align to an existing defense-in-depth strategy. This approach can strengthen resilience, but it can also add operational complexity for SOC teams. That’s why one year ago, we introduced the Microsoft Defender Integrated Cloud Email Security (ICES) vendor ecosystem, which is designed to simplify that complexity by integrating partner protections into Microsoft Defender.

Today, we’re continuing to expand the ICES vendor ecosystem by adding Proofpoint Core Email Protection API. Proofpoint joins existing members Darktrace, KnowBe4, Cisco, and VIPRE Security Group.

How joint customers benefit from a streamlined SOC experience in Microsoft Defender

The ICES ecosystem brings trusted third-party email security verdicts and telemetry into the Defender portal through an API-based integration model. This allows Microsoft Defender to acknowledge partner verdicts on messages, apply the highest-severity determination, and surface that information in the same investigation and response workflows security teams already use. The integration with Proofpoint Core Email Protection API is designed specifically for customers who have already chosen to deploy Proofpoint’s ICES solution alongside Microsoft Defender. It supports environments where customers run both solutions and want to reduce friction for their SOC teams. By integrating Proofpoint into the ICES ecosystem, customers can now preserve their existing security strategy while improving how investigations and response are carried out day to day.

"Organizations rely on both Microsoft and Proofpoint to protect their most critical communications and data. By extending Proofpoint’s interoperability across ICES, we’re delivering a more unified security experience that strengthens defense-in-depth and simplifies operations for our shared customers. This milestone reflects our commitment to joint customers worldwide.”

- Tom Corn, EVP and GM, Threat Protection Group at Proofpoint

Below we have outlined how Proofpoint’s ICES solution now integrates within Microsoft Defender:

Unified quarantine: Quarantine is the central place where suspicious, unwanted, or malicious messages are held so they do not remain in users’ mailboxes while analysts review them. With unified quarantine, teams can view and manage quarantined email from both Defender and supported ICES vendors in one experience. The benefit is less context switching, faster triage, and a more consistent response workflow because analysts do not need to jump between separate admin consoles to understand what was held and why. Figure 1: Emails quarantined by Proofpoint Core Email Protection API show up in the quarantine experience in Defender, alongside Defender-quarantined emails.

In Advanced Hunting, teams can query email events that include third-party detections to investigate patterns, validate coverage, and hunt for missed or emerging threats. And on the Email entity page, analysts can see message-level details and action history, including which product took action and what verdict was assigned. items.title: OpenBSD 8.0 Released With Major Security Hardening and Post-Quantum SSH Support
items.summary: OpenBSD 8.0 has been released with security fixes across its kernel, network services, firewall, and update tools, alongside experimental post-quantum SSH signature support. Released on October 20, 2026, the project’s 61st release includes OpenSSH 10.6 and LibreSSL 4.4.0, bringing stronger checks for untrusted data and changes to secure connection handling. The official release notes detail changes that address memory errors, unsafe file handling, and gaps in process isolation. For administrators, the update reaches beyond remote login security, covering web servers, mail delivery, DHCP services, virtual machines, and firmware installation. OpenSSH 10.6 includes experimental support for the composite mldsa44-ed25519 signature scheme, which combines ML-DSA 44 with Ed25519. The release also switches the scheme’s identifier from its OpenSSH-specific name to an IANA-allocated codepoint, a change that administrators testing earlier implementations should review. OpenBSD 8.0 Released This work concerns digital signatures rather than the initial introduction of post-quantum key exchange. As covered in OpenSSH 10.0’s security changes , that earlier release made hybrid ML-KEM and X25519 key agreement the default. OpenBSD 8.0 therefore builds on existing quantum-resistant connection protection rather than introducing it.mSSH hardening also includes turning off the LZ77 dictionary coder to avoid a potential side-channel leak. Developers corrected enforcement of ChannelTimeout and RekeyLimit settings and ensured the authorized_keys “restrict” option applies to tunnel forwarding. DisableForwarding now overrides PermitTunnel, tightening control over remote access features. Additional fixes address client memory errors, excessive expansion of compressed data, and validation of state passed between SSH server processes before and after authentication. Some key parsing and verification paths were also removed from the code exposed before login. On amd64 systems, OpenBSD now places the kernel’s direct memory map at a random location. The release also fixes kernel stack information leaks and removes an unprivileged kernel memory read and write vulnerability affecting the m88k 88100 data pipeline. These changes extend the security focus described in OpenBSD 7.7’s release coverage . Version 8.0 adds tighter pledge socket checks and limits file access for manual-page tools through unveil. The PF firewall receives fixes for out-of-bounds reads, connection counter races, and crafted reset packets that could incorrectly remove TCP state. Meanwhile, httpd rejects ambiguous request framing and obsolete folded headers. Relayd rejects duplicate Content-Length headers and removes Content-Length from chunked messages, reducing differences in how HTTP requests are handled. Firmware updates now verify signatures on local SHA256.sig files, restrict download sizes, and skip archive entries outside expected locations. Package installation no longer searches the current directory by default. At the same time, pax blocks malicious archives from extracting files outside the working directory. LibreSSL 4.4.0 makes X25519MLKEM768 the preferred TLS 1.3 group in libtls. It also fixes certificate checks, an OCSP responder authorization bypass, and excessive DTLS handshake buffering . Administrators should review compatibility changes, consult the linked upgrade documentation, and check release errata before deploying the update across production systems. items.title: Emperador Ransomware Group Claims to Have Stolen 3.9GB of Data from the Maker of Budweiser and Corona
items.summary: The Emperador ransomware group claims to have stolen 3.9GB of data from AB InBev and demands $1 million in Bitcoin, but the alleged breach remains unverified, with no company confirmation reported. The claim was discovered on October 25, 2026, at 03:22 UTC. The tracker lists the same day as the estimated attack date, but that does not establish when any unauthorized access began. Emperador says its collection includes 329,244 social-listening alerts, 2,510 corporate emails across AB InBev subsidiaries, around 19,000 access logs, and GBS portal records. The group also claims to hold internal public key infrastructure certificates and 3.2GB of Azure Blob assets . These figures describe the attackers’ account, not independently verified findings. “We hold 329,244 AB InBev social-listening alerts,” the group states in its posting, before listing the other records and its payment demand. The Azure assets account for most of the claimed data volume, but the listing does not explain their contents or how the group obtained them. Emperador Ransomware Claims AB InBev Data Theft According to Ransomware.live’s victim listing , the claims about corporate emails and access logs remain unclear, as the posting does not specify the type of email data involved or prove that attackers retained active access to company systems. The claimed certificate exposure needs careful interpretation. Microsoft’s X.509 certificate documentation explains that certificates contain public keys, not private keys. Therefore, possessing certificates alone does not prove an attacker can impersonate an internal service or decrypt protected information. The listing does not say whether private keys were obtained. Leak Screenshot (source: Ransomware.live ) The Azure claim lacks evidence of a compromised storage account, exposed token or key, or specific software flaw, and naming Azure files does not prove a Microsoft platform breach or explain how attackers accessed AB InBev’s environment. Separate Cyber Security News coverage of the Storm-3168 cloud attack documented compromised service identities and storage-key collection. Those findings illustrate why cloud identity evidence matters, but they should not be attributed to this alleged incident. The available claim does not establish that Emperador encrypted AB InBev systems, disrupted brewing operations, or affected product distribution. It also provides no verified count of affected people. Describing the event as a confirmed operational ransomware attack would go beyond the evidence currently available. That distinction also appears in Cyber Security News reporting on the PwC data-theft claim , which explains why a leak-site entry should not automatically be treated as proof of ransomware deployment. For now, the supported development is an extortion claim naming AB InBev. Confirmation requires evidence establishing the records’ authenticity, ownership, age, and source, alongside a clearer account of any unauthorized access and its impact. items.title: PHP Releases New Windows Build Security Updates to Fix Critical HTTP2Shell Vulnerability
items.summary: The PHP team has released updated Windows builds to fix a serious flaw known as HTTP2Shell . The new packages are PHP 8.5.12-1, 8.4.27-1, 8.3.36-1, and 8.2.35-1, and PHP announced them on October 26, 2026. Each build now includes Brotli 1.2.1, which fixes CVE-2026-111497. Windows users who run PHP should install these packages without delay. The flaw sits in Google’s Brotli library, a compression tool that many programs use to unpack data. It is an out-of-bounds write, which means the code writes data past the memory area it was meant to use. Node.js disclosed the bug in its security release on October 21, and researchers first called it Node2Shell . PHP HTTP2Shell Vulnerability As more software turned out to be affected, the name changed to HTTP2Shell. Google rates the issue with a CVSS v4.0 score of 9.2 out of 10. Depending on the setup, it can crash a program, expose memory contents, or let code run remotely without a login. PHP’s own advisory explains how the flaw reaches PHP on Windows. The vulnerable decoder can be reached through the cURL extension when automatic HTTP response decompression is turned on. This setting is off by default in cURL, according to the libcurl documentation. However, applications and HTTP client libraries can enable it. A PHP setup is therefore most at risk when it decodes Brotli data from sources it does not trust. The “-1” suffix in the new version numbers marks a Windows rebuild with updated dependencies, and the PHP runtime versions themselves do not change. Administrators should also check for a separate security release that PHP published on October 21. That release fixed two other critical flaws, CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619, which can allow remote code execution without a login. PHP 8.2 will reach end of life on December 31, 2026, so teams still on that branch should plan an upgrade to a supported version. The bug is not limited to PHP. Researchers have found it in Node.js, Python packages, .NET, FFmpeg, ClickHouse, and Apache Arrow. Microsoft and the maintainers of two Python packages have also shipped patches. Because so many products reuse Brotli, a version number alone may not show the full picture. Some vendors backport the fix into older releases, so a build can be safe even when its version number looks old. Security teams should start by confirming that every Windows PHP host runs one of the new -1 packages. They should also check any bundled Brotli libraries, since the fixed upstream versions are 1.0.10, 1.1.1 and 1.2.1. Teams that cannot patch right away should keep untrusted Brotli input away from production systems. The official PHP security advisory page and the Brotli 1.2.1 release notes on GitHub list the details, and the PHP Windows downloads page hosts the updated packages. For a wider view of the issue, read our earlier report on how HTTP2Shell reaches beyond web traffic into other software. Our coverage of the Node.js security updates also explains which release lines received fixes. Update defenses against new malware as soon as it appears. Integrate TI Feeds with data from 16K SOCs .

items.title: Pluralistic: Sovereign citizens, but for news (26 Oct 2026)
items.summary: Today's links Sovereign citizens, but for news : By reading the LA Times, you agree… Hey look at this : Delights to delectate. Object permanence : Patenting tax dodges; 6-word sf; Newscorp shareholders v Murdoch; Ancient German ophthalmology cult; Trolley problem is stupid; Trump's influence peddling to Chinese millionaire; Al Franken v binding arbitration; Yoga pants spite parade; Dems' secret Congressional committee; RIAA v your PC; "Going Under"; "Machine Man"; Aging goths; "Everfair"; Kremlin will destabilize Ukraine; FCC fronts for Big Cable; Straight Outta Vagina; Remixed TED Talk about remixing; Authoritarian debt. Upcoming appearances : Vienna, Kilkenny, Courtenay, Vancouver, Oxford, Sheffield, Virtual, Oxford, Montreal. Recent appearances : Where I've been. Latest books : You keep readin' em, I'll keep writin' 'em. Upcoming books : Like I said, I'll keep writin' 'em. Colophon : All the rest. Sovereign citizens, but for news ( permalink ) When it comes to terrible practices by website operators, it takes a lot to shock me. I literally wrote the book on the subject. But last night, I encountered a piece of genuinely appalling fuckery and I can't get it out of my head, because it's such a perfect storm of outrageous conduct and institutional decay. It happened when I followed a link to an LA Times article. Having lived in LA three times (and having been an Angeleno for a decade and counting this time around) I generally have warm feelings for the Times . The Times 's Festival of Books is a great event that I speak at most years, and I'm broadly happy to have a daily newspaper covering my city. That said, the Times has been chipping away at my goodwill for the past decade. First, there's the personal: after a Festival of Books appearance some years ago, the books editor approached me and asked if I'd contribute regular book reviews to the paper. I said yes, and then immediately my editor got laid off, reportedly so they could avoid giving him benefits that would come with seniority. I wrote several reviews for a new editor, though the paper never sent me a contract for any of them – or a payment! Many months (and published reviews) later, an editor I'd never had contact with at the paper got in touch to get the paperwork squared away, and the Times sent me a contract with broad, one-sided language that I would never sign onto. Given that they'd already published my work, there wasn't much they could do to make me sign the contract, so, after quite a lot of wrangling, I eventually got the offensive clauses removed and got paid (but I never got invited to write another review for them). To be honest, this is par for the course. The last time the New York Times asked me to write for them, they refused to remove some similar clauses from their contract (something they'd done previously), and the contracts person just ghosted me after a couple of volleys. A similar thing happened with the Washington Post the last time I wrote for them, except they (like the LAT ) published the work and then sent me a one-sided, manifestly unfair contract that I refused to sign. Given they'd already published the op-ed there wasn't anything they could do about it, so eventually I got a better contract and a payment (and again, that was the last time the Post asked me to write for them). Basically, there's an epidemic of bad legal terms sweeping the American media industry, and while the LA Times isn't the worst offender (at least they didn't ask me to assign any related patents, trademarks and copyrights to fictional characters, as Conde Nast does!), they're not what you'd call "writer-friendly" in their contracting terms. But again, that's hardly unique. If I disqualified news outlets because they tried to shift liability to, and grab rights from, their writers, I'd be left with damned few media outlets. But on the editorial side, the Times has a bunch of billionaire-shaped red flags. The paper's owner is the Trump-allied, severely AI-pilled biotech billionaire Patrick Soon-Shiong, whose editorial interference in the Times is comparable to Bezos's interference in the Post . Like Bezos, Soon-Shiong killed the paper's endorsement for Kamala Harris: https://www.nytimes.com/2024/10/26/us/los-angeles-times-endorsement-soon-shiong.html And I have my suspicions that Soon-Shiong might have been behind the layoff that killed Brian Merchant's beat as the country's first technology critic, from which perch Merchant assayed some acerbic, well-reasoned criticism of tech billionaires and AI: https://talkingbiznews.com/media-news/ex-la-times-tech-columnist-merchant-joining-ai-now-institute/ Again, that's not disqualifying. If I boycotted every newspaper owned by a reprehensible billionaire, I'd have to turn my back on e.g. the NYT with its morbidly wealthy, union-busting owners: https://www.thedailybeast.com/new-york-times-illegally-busted-union-campaign-national-labor-relations-board-alleges/ But unlike the NYT , the LA Times has followed the playbook of Alden Capital papers (like the Chicago Tribune ), shipping a skinnier paper with less original reporting at a higher price (which is why I canceled my subscription): https://archive.is/hOhpu But even that isn't disqualifying. Like the Tribune , the LAT still employs dedicated, talented reporters who do excellent work, which is how I came to be following a link to a recent article yesterday…and how I came to find myself confronted by an enshittificatory gambit that shocked even me. Here's what got me: when I visited the Times , I got a dickover that blocked all the content on the page until I clicked "Continue," and the text of that dickover is a breathtaking piece of enshittified legal fuckery: By continuing, you agree to our Terms of Service, which include arbitration and a class action waiver, and our Privacy Policy. You agree that we and our third-party vendors may collect and use your information, including through cookies, pixels and similar technologies, for the purposes set forth in our Privacy Policy such as personalizing your experience and ads. This is wildly illegal and incredibly immoral. The paper claims that by simply reading an article , you agree that you can never, ever sue them for virtually any reason , and that you have consented to effectively unlimited surveillance and commercial exploitation of your private data. It's hard to overstate how dangerous this kind of binding arbitration waiver is, but to give one example: Disney makes people who sign up for free trials of Disney Plus "consent" to one of these waivers. When a woman was killed by a Disney World restaurant that lied about the allergens in its food, the company told a judge that her grieving widower couldn't sue them because he'd waived that right by signing up for a trial of D+: https://lawreview.missouri.edu/infinite-arbitration-how-one-click-can-take-you-out-of-court-forever/ The company later backed off for that one specific case, but subsequently doubled down on binding arbitration. By putting an arbitration clause in its terms, the LAT could head off my right to sue them if they stiffed me on those reviews I wrote for them, Brian Merchant's right to sue them for wrongful termination, and your right to sue them if you get run over by a newspaper delivery van. Then there's the privacy clause: the LAT is a California paper, and in California, we have the CCPA, a reasonably good privacy law. Under the CCPA, privacy waivers have to be explicit, informed and can be withdrawn at any time. What's more, the CCPA has broad prohibitions against "dark patterns" that this dickover almost certainly violates: https://cppa.ca.gov/announcements/2024/20240904.html In theory, there's a way to avoid all of this: you could just use the "Kill Sticky" bookmarklet or an adblock filter to block or dismiss the dickover without ever clicking "continue": https://pluralistic.net/2026/07/21/dickovers/#block-element But this is an industrial strength dickover; it uses advanced tricks to block existing dickover killers, likely a combination of shadow DOM and an "important" scroll-lock in the html. Like I say, this shocks the conscience. Under this standard, the Times 's reporters could find themselves bound to legal "agreements" with the companies they investigate online that could interfere with their reporting. Just as bad is how these illegal measures mislead the Times 's readership on two of the most important consumer issues facing Californians (and all internet users) today. The very idea that everyone who reads a single article on a newspaper's website "consents" to an 8,865-word privacy policy (that would take 53-67 minutes to read according to Firefox's "Reader Mode" estimate) is a bad joke: https://www.latimes.com/privacy-policy The joke gets even worse when you add in the 7,103-word Terms of Service (estimated read: 41-50 minutes): https://www.latimes.com/terms-of-service So what can you do? Sovereign citizens, but for news (permalink)

When it comes to terrible practices by website operators, it takes a lot to shock me. I literally wrote the book on the subject. But last night, I encountered a piece of genuinely appalling fuckery and I can't get it out of my head, because it's such a perfect storm of outrageous conduct and institutional decay.

It happened when I followed a link to an LA Times article. Having lived in LA three times (and having been an Angeleno for a decade and counting this time around) I generally have warm feelings for the Times. The Times's Festival of Books is a great event that I speak at most years, and I'm broadly happy to have a daily newspaper covering my city.

That said, the Times has been chipping away at my goodwill for the past decade. First, there's the personal: after a Festival of Books appearance some years ago, the books editor approached me and asked if I'd contribute regular book reviews to the paper. I said yes, and then immediately my editor got laid off, reportedly so they could avoid giving him benefits that would come with seniority.

I wrote several reviews for a new editor, though the paper never sent me a contract for any of them – or a payment! Many months (and published reviews) later, an editor I'd never had contact with at the paper got in touch to get the paperwork squared away, and the Times sent me a contract with broad, one-sided language that I would never sign onto.

Given that they'd already published my work, there wasn't much they could do to make me sign the contract, so, after quite a lot of wrangling, I eventually got the offensive clauses removed and got paid (but I never got invited to write another review for them).

To be honest, this is par for the course. The last time the New York Times asked me to write for them, they refused to remove some similar clauses from their contract (something they'd done previously), and the contracts person just ghosted me after a couple of volleys.

A similar thing happened with the Washington Post the last time I wrote for them, except they (like the LAT) published the work and then sent me a one-sided, manifestly unfair contract that I refused to sign. Given they'd already published the op-ed there wasn't anything they could do about it, so eventually I got a better contract and a payment (and again, that was the last time the Post asked me to write for them).

Basically, there's an epidemic of bad legal terms sweeping the American media industry, and while the LA Times isn't the worst offender (at least they didn't ask me to assign any related patents, trademarks and copyrights to fictional characters, as Conde Nast does!), they're not what you'd call "writer-friendly" in their contracting terms.

But again, that's hardly unique. If I disqualified news outlets because they tried to shift liability to, and grab rights from, their writers, I'd be left with damned few media outlets.

But on the editorial side, the Times has a bunch of billionaire-shaped red flags. The paper's owner is the Trump-allied, severely AI-pilled biotech billionaire Patrick Soon-Shiong, whose editorial interference in the Times is comparable to Bezos's interference in the Post. Like Bezos, Soon-Shiong killed the paper's endorsement for Kamala Harris:

https://www.nytimes.com/2024/10/26/us/los-angeles-times-endorsement-soon-shiong.html

And I have my suspicions that Soon-Shiong might have been behind the layoff that killed Brian Merchant's beat as the country's first technology critic, from which perch Merchant assayed some acerbic, well-reasoned criticism of tech billionaires and AI:

https://talkingbiznews.com/media-news/ex-la-times-tech-columnist-merchant-joining-ai-now-institute/

Again, that's not disqualifying. If I boycotted every newspaper owned by a reprehensible billionaire, I'd have to turn my back on e.g. the NYT with its morbidly wealthy, union-busting owners:

https://www.thedailybeast.com/new-york-times-illegally-busted-union-campaign-national-labor-relations-board-alleges/

But unlike the NYT, the LA Times has followed the playbook of Alden Capital papers (like the Chicago Tribune), shipping a skinnier paper with less original reporting at a higher price (which is why I canceled my subscription):

https://archive.is/hOhpu

But even that isn't disqualifying. Like the Tribune, the LAT still employs dedicated, talented reporters who do excellent work, which is how I came to be following a link to a recent article yesterday…and how I came to find myself confronted by an enshittificatory gambit that shocked even me.

Here's what got me: when I visited the Times, I got a dickover that blocked all the content on the page until I clicked "Continue," and the text of that dickover is a breathtaking piece of enshittified legal fuckery:

By continuing, you agree to our Terms of Service, which include arbitration and a class action waiver, and our Privacy Policy. You agree that we and our third-party vendors may collect and use your information, including through cookies, pixels and similar technologies, for the purposes set forth in our Privacy Policy such as personalizing your experience and ads.

This is wildly illegal and incredibly immoral. The paper claims that by simply reading an article, you agree that you can never, ever sue them for virtually any reason, and that you have consented to effectively unlimited surveillance and commercial exploitation of your private data.

It's hard to overstate how dangerous this kind of binding arbitration waiver is, but to give one example: Disney makes people who sign up for free trials of Disney Plus "consent" to one of these waivers. When a woman was killed by a Disney World restaurant that lied about the allergens in its food, the company told a judge that her grieving widower couldn't sue them because he'd waived that right by signing up for a trial of D+:

https://lawreview.missouri.edu/infinite-arbitration-how-one-click-can-take-you-out-of-court-forever/

The company later backed off for that one specific case, but subsequently doubled down on binding arbitration. By putting an arbitration clause in its terms, the LAT could head off my right to sue them if they stiffed me on those reviews I wrote for them, Brian Merchant's right to sue them for wrongful termination, and your right to sue them if you get run over by a newspaper delivery van.

Then there's the privacy clause: the LAT is a California paper, and in California, we have the CCPA, a reasonably good privacy law. Under the CCPA, privacy waivers have to be explicit, informed and can be withdrawn at any time. What's more, the CCPA has broad prohibitions against "dark patterns" that this dickover almost certainly violates:

https://cppa.ca.gov/announcements/2024/20240904.html

In theory, there's a way to avoid all of this: you could just use the "Kill Sticky" bookmarklet or an adblock filter to block or dismiss the dickover without ever clicking "continue":

https://pluralistic.net/2026/07/21/dickovers/#block-element

But this is an industrial strength dickover; it uses advanced tricks to block existing dickover killers, likely a combination of shadow DOM and an "important" scroll-lock in the html.

Like I say, this shocks the conscience. Under this standard, the Times's reporters could find themselves bound to legal "agreements" with the companies they investigate online that could interfere with their reporting. items.title: Introducing a Voluntary Exit Offer
items.summary: Amy Coleman, Executive Vice President and Chief People Officer, shared the below communication with Microsoft employees today. Today, we’re introducing a new Voluntary Exit Offer (VEO) to eligible employees within participating organizations. This offer gives eligible employees who may be considering a future outside the company a new choice to make that transition now with support. It also gives participating organizations another way to adapt their workforce to changing needs. The Voluntary Exit Offer reflects an important part of how we’re evolving our approach to change: creating greater flexibility and, where possible, more ways for employees to shape their next chapter. This builds on what we learned earlier this year through the Voluntary Retirement Program. What employees should know This offer will be available to eligible employees in participating teams in Canada, India, the United Kingdom and the United States at level 70 and below . This is a time-limited, voluntary program that gives those who are eligible the opportunity to leave Microsoft with financial support and career planning resources. Some organizations are providing the Voluntary Exit Offer, and some are not. Participation varies based on each business’s priorities, customer commitments and workforce needs. Eligible employees will receive an email with a link to their Voluntary Exit Offer details within the next few hours. Looking ahead The Voluntary Exit Offer is new for us. We’ll learn from it. At the same time, we’ll keep helping people focus on the work that matters most, build new skills and, where it makes sense, find new opportunities across Microsoft. There is no one-size-fits-all approach for every team or every employee. These are a few of the ways we’re trying to meet different business needs while continuing to create opportunities for our own people to grow and contribute. My promise is to continue to provide clarity, listen and learn and keep improving. Thank you for everything you continue to do for our customers, Microsoft and for one another. Amy This Viva Engage post has been edited slightly for external use.

items.title: Check Point Launches Firewall-as-a-Subscription as Cybersecurity Budgets Face Growing Pressure
items.summary: Check Point Software Technologies has announced the launch of Firewall-as-a-Subscription, a new offering designed to make advanced AI-powered network security more accessible to organisations without requiring a significant upfront hardware investment. The new subscription model gives businesses access to Check Point Force Firewalls, AI-powered threat prevention and agentic security management through predictable monthly or annual payments. The offering is designed to help organisations modernise their network defences while managing increasingly constrained cybersecurity budgets. The announcement comes as businesses face growing financial pressures, with inflation and higher borrowing costs forcing many to delay infrastructure upgrades. According to the IANS Research and Artico Search 2026 Security Budget Benchmark , the median cybersecurity budget remained unchanged this year, with 55% of CISOs reporting flat or declining budgets. Although 64% requested additional funding, just 45% received an increase. These financial constraints are emerging at a time when AI adoption is introducing new challenges for network security, including the need to inspect AI-generated traffic, protect AI applications and monitor autonomous agents. Check Point’s Firewall-as-a-Subscription aims to address these challenges by removing the need for large capital investments, allowing organisations to access advanced security capabilities through a subscription-based model. The offering builds on Check Point’s R82.20 release, introduced in July 2026, which brought AI Network Firewall capabilities designed to inspect AI traffic, protect AI applications and help govern AI agents at the network layer. The subscription includes Check Point Force Firewalls, with capacity and pricing based on the threat prevention throughput required by each organisation. Customers also receive AI-powered threat prevention, including SandBlast technology, which Check Point claims achieves a 99.9% block rate against zero-day attacks. Additional features include Live Updates, which enable security updates without reboots or downtime, and Smart-1 cloud-based agentic management. The package also includes 24/7 premium support and professional services credits to assist with activities such as migrating firewall policies from other vendors. Under the three-year subscription, organisations can increase their firewall throughput as their requirements evolve, with the option to move to new hardware after 36 months. Pete Finalle, Research Manager, Security and Trust at IDC, commented on the growing demand for more flexible security purchasing models. “Organizations of all sizes face the same AI-driven threats, but for many, capital budget cycles often force them to delay firewall refreshes or buy more capacity than they need,” he said. “Consumption models that turn on-premises security hardware into a predictable operating expense, and let organizations scale protection as their needs grow, can help close that gap. We expect demand for this kind of flexibility to rise as AI adoption increases the traffic and risk networks must handle.” The subscription model could also provide opportunities for channel partners to help customers progress firewall refresh projects that have been delayed by capital expenditure restrictions. Avi Rembaum, President Global Technical Sales at Check Point Software Technologies, said: “Every organization is adopting AI, and every organization deserves the same level of protection, whatever its size or budget. “With Firewall-as-a-Subscription, we are making our most advanced AI security, threat prevention and agentic management available through one simple subscription, so organizations can secure their AI transformation today.” Check Point Firewall-as-a-Subscription will be available from 1 November 2026 through Check Point’s partner network, with monthly and annual payment options.

items.title: Researchers Use AI Agents to Breach Anthropic’s Internal Systems in Just 12 Hours
items.summary: Cybersecurity startup Cathedral says its AI agents found routes into Anthropic’s internal business systems in less than 12 hours, exposing how fast automated security tools can find and chain flaws across connected services. The work took place through Anthropic’s program for outside researchers, making this an authorized security test rather than a criminal attack, according to The Washington Post. Anthropic Internal System Breach According to reporting from The Washington Post , the agents did not break Anthropic’s core AI models or exploit the company’s own code. Instead, Cathedral said they used weaknesses in unnamed third-party software used for administrative and sales work. Once inside, researchers reached meeting transcripts, salary and job-offer details, and internal Slack talks about Anthropic’s advanced AI models. Anthropic confirmed in a statement to The Washington Post that Cathedral accessed a limited group of sales, human resources, and IT systems. Those systems held business contact information for some customers and partners, along with basic user account records. However, customer prompts, Claude responses, source code, and model weights were not accessed. This limit matters because model weights and source code are among an AI company’s most sensitive assets. Anthropic also said its monitoring tools flagged some of Cathedral’s actions before the startup reported them. The company ended the access on the same day, disabled the affected business software, and restored it only after the vendors confirmed that fixes were ready. Anthropic said it found no evidence that anyone outside Cathedral had used the weaknesses. The two sides disagree on parts of the test. Anthropic said Cathedral did not fully follow its bug bounty rules because it failed to disclose all activity within the company’s systems. Cathedral said it kept data access to the minimum needed for responsible research. The vendors behind the affected software were also notified, but their names and the exact flaws were withheld to reduce the risk of misuse. The case shows why third-party application security is now a major concern for AI labs. A company may protect model infrastructure while connected HR, sales, identity, and collaboration tools create other paths into sensitive business data. Security teams should map every software connection, limit application permissions, review OAuth tokens, monitor unusual account behavior, and quickly remove access that is no longer needed. It also shows how AI agents can compress security testing. Agents can scan systems, test paths, run tools, and review results with less waiting between steps. Cyber Security News has previously reported how AI agents can automate the cyber kill chain and how Claude exploited software flaws during controlled evaluations . These cases do not mean humans are removed. Researchers still set the scope, judge findings, and control disclosure. Cathedral is only months old, but it has gained attention. The company was co-founded by Gavin Kliger, Luke Farritor, Marko Elez, and Jack Stein, all former DOGE staffers. Kliger served as the Pentagon’s chief data officer. Reuters reported in July that Cathedral raised $160 million at a $1.4 billion valuation, with Andreessen Horowitz and Sequoia Capital leading the round. A senior Trump administration official told The Washington Post that three federal agencies had contracted with Cathedral and that the government was working with the startup on hostile AI scenarios. items.title: Popcorn Time’s forgotten updater left millions of devices exposed to hijacking
items.summary: You may have forgotten about Popcorn Time. Unfortunately, its updater didn’t forget about your device. Security researchers have intervened to disable an abandoned update mechanism in Time4Popcorn, a version of the once-popular streaming app. If left running in the background, the updater could have allowed attackers to take control of Windows and Mac computers, even if their owners hadn’t opened the app in years. Eye Security estimates that the vulnerable updater was present on millions of devices worldwide, including 2.5–3 million Windows computers and around 250,000–350,000 Macs. Popcorn Time made watching movies and TV shows through BitTorrent look more like browsing Netflix. Rather than making users find torrent files and open them in a separate client, it wrapped the process in a familiar streaming-style interface. Amid concerns about copyright infringement and its possible consequences, the original developers abandoned it shortly after its launch in 2014. But because its source code was publicly available, other developers could pick it up and create their own versions, known as forks. One of those was Time4Popcorn, which was also distributed under the name “Popcorn Time.” That shared branding matters because people may have installed the affected software without ever seeing the Time4Popcorn name. The problem at hand Time4Popcorn was eventually abandoned too. But its update infrastructure was left behind, and at some point the domains associated with the software became available for others to register. In other words, the people maintaining the software had gone away. The software’s ability to accept instructions had not. Time4Popcorn’s updater used unencrypted HTTP connections and accepted executable updates without checking digital signatures to verify their authenticity. So, someone who controlled an update domain or was able to tamper with the unencrypted traffic could supply their own program instead. That combination created a remote code execution vulnerability, tracked as CVE-2026-30612 , which could let an attacker run malicious software on a device. An attacker wouldn’t need to persuade someone to watch a movie or click a suspicious attachment. The forgotten updater could do the work for them. Although Android was affected too, users had an extra layer of protection. Its updater checked for updates when the application was opened, but installing an attacker-supplied APK required the user to approve the installation. items.summary_html:
You may have forgotten about Popcorn Time. Unfortunately, its updater didn’t forget about your device.

Security researchers have intervened to disable an abandoned update mechanism in Time4Popcorn, a version of the once-popular streaming app. If left running in the background, the updater could have allowed attackers to take control of Windows and Mac computers, even if their owners hadn’t opened the app in years.

Eye Security estimates that the vulnerable updater was present on millions of devices worldwide, including 2.5–3 million Windows computers and around 250,000–350,000 Macs.

Popcorn Time made watching movies and TV shows through BitTorrent look more like browsing Netflix. Rather than making users find torrent files and open them in a separate client, it wrapped the process in a familiar streaming-style interface.

Amid concerns about copyright infringement and its possible consequences, the original developers abandoned it shortly after its launch in 2014. But because its source code was publicly available, other developers could pick it up and create their own versions, known as forks.

One of those was Time4Popcorn, which was also distributed under the name “Popcorn Time.” That shared branding matters because people may have installed the affected software without ever seeing the Time4Popcorn name.

The problem at hand

Time4Popcorn was eventually abandoned too. But its update infrastructure was left behind, and at some point the domains associated with the software became available for others to register.

In other words, the people maintaining the software had gone away. The software’s ability to accept instructions had not. Time4Popcorn’s updater used unencrypted HTTP connections and accepted executable updates without checking digital signatures to verify their authenticity. So, someone who controlled an update domain or was able to tamper with the unencrypted traffic could supply their own program instead.

That combination created a remote code execution vulnerability, tracked as CVE-2026-30612, which could let an attacker run malicious software on a device. An attacker wouldn’t need to persuade someone to watch a movie or click a suspicious attachment. The forgotten updater could do the work for them.

Although Android was affected too, users had an extra layer of protection. Its updater checked for updates when the application was opened, but installing an attacker-supplied APK required the user to approve the installation. It was not the same silent, background takeover route researchers found on Windows and macOS.

What the researchers did

Eye Security registered an abandoned update domain and used the vulnerable mechanism to distribute an update that disabled the updater itself. On Windows, it stopped and disabled the service; on macOS, it prevented the update process from starting. The researchers say their intervention did not delete users’ files or collect host data.

By March 2026, Eye Security reported more than two million downloads of its updater-disabling fix, and update requests to its domains had fallen by 98%. Later that month, it transferred the 15 domains it controlled to the nonprofit Shadowserver Foundation.

Researchers could not remotely disable the Android updater in the same way. And the desktop application still contained other weaknesses, including an obsolete Chrome engine dating from 2014 and disabled sandbox protections, which normally help contain malicious code.

What users should do

If you used Popcorn Time years ago, check the devices on which you installed it. Don’t assume that no longer using an application means its background components have stopped running.

  • Check your list of installed applications for Popcorn Time or Time4Popcorn. Pay particular attention to older Windows PCs, Macs, and Android devices where you may have forgotten about installing it. The affected fork was distributed under both names.
  • Remove the old application. There is no vendor security update for the abandoned Time4Popcorn software. Disabling the updater addresses one vulnerability, not the application’s other security weaknesses.
  • On Windows and macOS, check that the background updater is no longer running. Eye Security identifies the Windows component as Updater.exe, normally inside a Popcorn Time folder under Program Files or Program Files (x86), running through a service called Update Service. On macOS, the component is /Library/PrivilegedHelperTools/PT.updd, with a launch daemon at /Library/LaunchDaemons/PT.updd.plist. Its advisory provides instructions for disabling these components if needed.
  • On Android, uninstall the affected app rather than accepting an update prompt from it. The updater is part of the main application and cannot easily be disabled separately.
  • Use an up-to-date, real-time anti-malware solution to detect and block any attempts to install malware on your devices.

As we saw recently, cybercriminals can use software updates to distribute malware. Remove abandoned apps and check for any background updaters they leave behind.
