items.title: Can’t Patch PHP2Shell Yet? Build a Stopgap with the Controls You Own
items.summary: PHP2Shell comes with a clear instruction: update PHP. Fixed releases exist for supported branches, and Qualys customers can identify PHP installations using network scans, Cloud Agents, container assessments, and Deep Scan where supported, while assessing exposed web applications and APIs with Qualys TotalAppSec. Patching at this scale still takes time. In Qualys telemetry, only 199,000 of the 156 million PHP package installations with a known version had been patched during the first 12 hours after disclosure. Those first days are where mitigations and compensating controls earn their place. They reduce risk while updates roll out, and the right visibility shows which servers need attention first. Our PHP2Shell guide covers detection and fixed versions. Here is how to bridge the gap between disclosure and patch. Start with Qualys Mitigation Qualys provides a configuration-level mitigation for PHP2Shell based on PHP’s guidance and insights from the Qualys Threat Research Unit. It disables session upload progress and hardens related session-handling configuration on supported hosts. This reduces exposure to the confirmed session-lifecycle attack path without requiring application-code changes. It does not eliminate every exploitation path associated with the two CVEs. Applications that depend on upload-progress functionality should be tested after the change. Configuration-level, with restart verification . The mitigation applies configuration changes and automatically restarts the PHP service. Review the execution logs and restart the service manually if a restart is still required. Confirm that every affected PHP worker has picked up the new configuration. Verified, not assumed. After the restart, Qualys checks the effective configuration to confirm the setting is active and not overridden elsewhere. With or without an agent. Customers with vulnerable detections can select Mitigate Now from their dashboards. For appliances, DMZ servers, and legacy hosts that cannot run a Cloud Agent, the same mitigation script is available in the Custom Assessment and Remediation (CAR) library in TruRisk Eliminate and runs directly on scanner-based hosts. Ready when the patch is. You can deploy supported vendor patches through TruRisk Eliminate. Qualys reports a High patch reliability rating for these updates and no OS reboot requirement for this PHP package update. Restart every service that loads PHP and verify that its workers are running the patched build. Mitigation reduces risk in the interim. Updating remains the only complete fix. Add Layers from the Security Stack You Already Run The tools already in your environment can work alongside the mitigation, each at a different point in the attack path. Network and application protection: WAF and IPS. Vendors including Akamai, Cloudflare, F5, Palo Alto Networks, Fortinet, and Check Point have published PHP2Shell protections. Coverage varies by product, CVE, signature, and configuration. These protections can block known exploit requests; some, including Cloudflare’s, also inspect and block malicious responses. Keep signatures current and confirm that the relevant traffic is inspected and blocking is enabled. Cloudflare has reported attempts to bypass its protections, so treat these controls as additional layers while patching proceeds. After exploitation: EDR. Endpoint controls can provide visibility into suspicious child processes, malicious command execution, and web-shell deployment. CrowdStrike Falcon and Cortex XDR document PHP2Shell-related post-exploitation protections. For Microsoft Defender for Endpoint and other tools, verify the applicable platform support and enabled policies before claiming specific coverage. Signatures covering both CVEs: Akamai 3000991; Cloudflare seven managed rules; F5 BIG-IP 200204113, 200103697, 200204115; FortiWeb 1002017614, 1002017615; Palo Alto Networks 543004, 97622 to 97625; FortiGate 62657, 62658; Check Point CPAI-2026-15172, 15184, 15224; Trend Vision One 1012749, 1012754. Endpoint policies are listed for CrowdStrike Falcon, Microsoft Defender for Endpoint, Cortex XDR, SentinelOne and Cybereason. Note: Rule and policy IDs are as published by each vendor in October 2026; confirm them in your console. The endpoint policies act after exploitation and are mapped to the attacker’s next step, not to the CVEs themselves, so verify each one fires for your PHP worker. Compensating controls reduce risk; updating PHP remains the only complete fix. Give Your Controls Credit in Qualys ETM Two servers can run the same unpatched PHP build and carry very different risk. One sits behind a WAF rule that names both CVEs, with EDR watching its web server process. The other faces the internet with nothing in front of it. A version-based check can report the same vulnerability on both assets, even though their exposure and compensating controls differ. Qualys ETM is being extended to close that gap. It arrives in three steps: Recommendations on every finding. ETM will show which applicable third-party controls can reduce exposure for each vulnerability, so teams know what to enable and where. Controls reflected in the score. Controls that are in place will lower a finding’s QVSS score to reflect your actual defenses, shown as the Environmental score, so remediation queues focus on what still needs attention. Action from the same platform. Teams will be able to apply third-party mitigations through TruRisk Eliminate, from the platform that found the exposure. Validate the Tested Entry Point with TruConfirm TruConfirm helps validate indicators of the tested PHP2Shell entry point. According to Qualys’s PHP2Shell guide , its benign probe checks for behavior indicating that the entry point is reachable and the upload-progress mitigation is absent, without creating files, executing code, or applying memory pressure. Qualys reports that, in one customer environment with 1,539 assets running PHP, TruConfirm returned positive validation results for 25 assets. These findings help prioritize investigation and remediation. A negative result does not establish that every exploitation path is closed. After mitigation or patching, repeat the validation and separately verify the effective configuration, installed packages, and running PHP workers. Where to Start Use QID 45110 to support PHP discovery, then use the applicable vulnerability detection QIDs and software inventory to assess assets in scope. Use TruConfirm results alongside internet exposure and business criticality to prioritize remediation. Apply the supported Qualys mitigation workflow to systems awaiting an update, using agent-based or scanner-based execution as applicable. Verify the effective configuration and required restarts.Keep applicable WAF, IPS, and EDR protections enabled and current as additional layers. Deploy the appropriate PHP or vendor update, restart every service that loads PHP, verify the running patched build, and repeat the relevant validation checks. Compensating controls buy valuable time, but they do not remove the flaw. Keep tracking every system until it is patched. Not a Qualys customer yet? items.title: Hacker Exploits Critical PHP2Shell Flaws to Win $2,000 Bitcoin Challenge, Releases PoC
items.summary: A security researcher known online as killa has won a public Bitcoin challenge by using two critical PHP flaws to reach a test server. The winning run took 19.28 hours. The prize pot was 0.02511679 BTC, worth $2,021.22 at the time of the win on October 25, 2026, at 15:47 UTC. The researcher then published a proof of concept (PoC) on GitHub. The challenge ran on stealmybitcoin.com. The site used unpatched PHP and held a wallet key behind a remote code execution test, which means the goal was to run commands on the server from the outside. Donations pushed the prize from $500 to more than $2,000 while the test ran. The creator said early tries failed because the server first served static files through PHP’s command-line mode, which skipped the bugs. After the site moved to a real PHP page, the test became possible. PHP2Shell Flaws Exploited The bugs are tracked as CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619 , and the group is called PHP2Shell. Both carry a CVSS v4.0 score of 9.2, which is rated critical. The first bug can corrupt memory during cleanup after an out-of-memory condition. The second lets data left by an earlier request in a shared worker be reused by a later request. PHP released fixes on October 21, 2026, in versions 8.5.12, 8.4.27, 8.3.36 and 8.2.35. Google’s guidance says the affected range covers PHP 5.4 through 8.5.11. Older branches such as 8.1 and earlier no longer get official fixes, so those sites need to move to a supported version. The public script uses two memory leaks. The first leak reveals a heap address, and the second reveals a PHP code address. With both addresses, a final request places a forged structure in memory that leads PHP to call its system function. The script then prints a random test marker, the user ID, and the hash of the flag program. The write-up also shows the limits of the work. The script was built and tested against a local lab copy, not the live site, and it succeeded in about seven of ten lab runs. The author admits that the full live request was not captured. The recovered key also did not match the advertised prize address, and the author called that a mistake on the creator’s side. Public exploit code is now available , and hacking activity started before the patches. Amazon reported attempts dating back to October 17, four days before the fixes. Sophos said it blocked attempts to deliver Potassium, a likely Mirai botnet variant, but it found no proof of a successful compromise. Upgrading to a patched PHP release is the only full fix. Firewall rules and configuration changes may reduce risk, but they do not close the flaws. After upgrading, restart services and confirm that the active workers run the new build, because bundled runtimes and containers may still use old code. For more background, read our earlier coverage of the PHP2Shell vulnerability and public PoC and the PHP emergency patch release . Update defenses against new malware as soon as it appears. items.title: Our Response To The eMudhra Key Disclosure Incident
items.summary: The Go Blog Our Response To The eMudhra Key Disclosure Incident Roland Shoemaker, on behalf of the Go Security team 26 October 2026 On October 19, the Go team initiated an expedited security release to protect Go users and their applications from a critical public key infrastructure (PKI) compromise involving certificates issued by eMudhra. Within approximately seven and a half hours of being notified, we shipped a targeted patch, which was included in our first-ever URGENT track security release. Here is the context behind the incident, why Go stepped in at the runtime level to protect our users and how our incident response unfolded. eMudhra Incident On October 17, Mozilla added eight intermediate certificates (six used for TLS, and two used for code signing) issued by a root certificate controlled by eMudhra to OneCRL, effectively blocking their usage in Firefox. Soon after, a number of security researchers noticed this and began investigating what might’ve caused this. On October 19, the Go Security team was made aware of these investigations and their conclusions, which showed that the keys associated with these intermediates were trivially weak, allowing recovery of the private keys in microseconds. Due to the fact that the eMudhra root certificate was present in most trusted root programs, recovering the private keys would allow any attacker to sign arbitrary TLS certificates for any domain name, without the usual requirement to show proof of control of said domain name. This would allow an attacker to man-in-the-middle (MITM) TLS connections and present a valid certificate for a domain name they did not control, effectively allowing them to impersonate any TLS server the targeted machine attempted to connect to. Go ships a TLS certificate verifier in the standard library. When users use net/http or crypto/tls to connect to a TLS service, the verifier is called to check if the certificates the other side of the connection presents are valid. On Windows and macOS we delegate these checks to the platform APIs, and on Linux, which lacks platform APIs, we use our own verifier implementation. Since Linux does not have a uniform built-in mechanism to handle revocation checking, and in order to provide a timely fix for users on other platforms that might not receive platform updates, we decided the best way to protect Go users was to do an URGENT track security release which similarly removed trust. Incident Timeline A typical Go security release follows a multi-day process, with advanced pre-announcements in order to allow those who rely on Go to prepare. In this case, because we believed that private key exposure was imminent, our team chose to use the URGENT track for the first time in order to ship protections before active public exploitation could begin. 11:45 PDT Our Security team was alerted by an independent external researcher, citing unreported actions by Mozilla and other organizations to remove trust in eight eMudhra intermediates. It became clear quickly that this was due to weak private keys they used. 12:30 PDT Mozilla independently reported the issue to our Security team, confirming the issue, and asking that we not immediately disclose the issue, but encouraging us to release a fix as soon as possible. 14:00 PDT We finalized a patch which blocked the usage of certificates which chained to the compromised intermediates, and thanks to the researcher who initially alerted us to the issue, had a set of certificates signed using the recovered keys to test against. 15:00 PDT We began the process to release minor Go versions 1.27.3 and 1.26.10 containing our patch. Due to the urgent nature of this issue and its exploitability, and with the belief that the private keys would likely become publicly known within hours, we decided an immediate release was the most prudent option. 19:13 PDT We finalized the release and announced it publicly. At this time the underlying issue was still not widely known. In an effort to give other defenders a chance to protect as many users as possible without revealing to attackers how the issue could be exploited, our patch and communications were somewhat opaque, warning users that we were “blocking trust in a small set of intermediate certificates due to specific security concerns around their operation” and urging users to immediately upgrade to this release. In under seven and a half hours from initial notification, patched Go releases were live worldwide, giving users everything they needed to secure their deployments before the keys became public. By the morning of October 20, numerous independent researchers had publicly disclosed the weak keys. Lessons Learned and Future Improvements This was our first ever URGENT track security release, and during the release process we ran into a number of issues which caused the release to take longer than expected. While we are happy we were able to get a release out the same day we were notified of the issue, in the modern security environment we feel that we should be able to provide releases in a more compressed timeline. The issues we ran into caused our release process to take just under four and a quarter hours from start to finish. These issues had previously not been problematic, since the typical release process is split up over a number of days. We’ve subsequently made a number of changes to improve our release efficiency, which should significantly reduce the time it takes us to push out a release, enhancing our ability to quickly respond to urgent security threats. PRIVATE track security fixes are pre-announced three to seven days before their release. URGENT track fixes happen on a shorter time schedule, but we could have pre-announced the upcoming release when we began the release process, giving users at least a few hours to prepare. While on Windows and macOS we rely on the revocation mechanisms the platform APIs provide, on Linux we don’t currently have a similar mechanism. The lack of this support was one of our major drivers to issue an expedited security release, as we did not want to leave Linux users exposed to this issue longer than was necessary. Hence we are planning on prioritizing work to bring parity to revocation support on Linux, to help mitigate this class of issues in the future. Part of this work will involve investigating adding support for the upki project, which aims to “provide reliable, privacy-preserving and efficient certificate revocation” for Linux (see issue #82402 ). Upgrading and Verifying Your Deployments If you run Go binaries which interact with network services using TLS (such as directly via net/http or crypto/tls or via a dependency such as gRPC), ensure you are running on the latest minor releases. Binaries rebuilt with Go 1.27.3 and 1.26.10 will automatically reject certificates issued by the compromised eMudhra intermediates. You can verify your current toolchain version using go version and you can check the version of Go a binary was built with using go version -m . The govulncheck tool can also be used to determine if a binary is affected by this issue: $ GOTOOLCHAIN=go1.27.3+auto go install golang.org/x/vuln/cmd/govulncheck@latest $ govulncheck -mode=binary Securing Go Deployments Everywhere For us, securing Go and its users extends beyond fixing direct security vulnerabilities in the runtime and libraries we ship. In order to keep the ecosystem secure, we believe we also need to provide users with the right tools to write secure software, look towards the future of cryptographic algorithms and protocols, and proactively respond to ecosystem wide issues when we can. We are grateful to the independent security researchers and the Mozilla security team for this rapid notification and coordination during this incident. Our Security team was alerted by an independent external researcher, citing unreported actions by Mozilla and other organizations to remove trust in eight eMudhra intermediates. It became clear quickly that this was due to weak private keys they used.

12:30 PDT

Mozilla independently reported the issue to our Security team, confirming the issue, and asking that we not immediately disclose the issue, but encouraging us to release a fix as soon as possible.

14:00 PDT

We finalized a patch which blocked the usage of certificates which chained to the compromised intermediates, and thanks to the researcher who initially alerted us to the issue, had a set of certificates signed using the recovered keys to test against.

15:00 PDT

We began the process to release minor Go versions 1.27.3 and 1.26.10 containing our patch. Due to the urgent nature of this issue and its exploitability, and with the belief that the private keys would likely become publicly known within hours, we decided an immediate release was the most prudent option.

19:13 PDT

We finalized the release and announced it publicly. At this time the underlying issue was still not widely known. In an effort to give other defenders a chance to protect as many users as possible without revealing to attackers how the issue could be exploited, our patch and communications were somewhat opaque, warning users that we were “blocking trust in a small set of intermediate certificates due to specific security concerns around their operation” and urging users to immediately upgrade to this release.

In under seven and a half hours from initial notification, patched Go releases were live worldwide, giving users everything they needed to secure their deployments before the keys became public.

By the morning of October 20, numerous independent researchers had publicly disclosed the weak keys.

Lessons Learned and Future Improvements

This was our first ever URGENT track security release, and during the release process we ran into a number of issues which caused the release to take longer than expected.

While we are happy we were able to get a release out the same day we were notified of the issue, in the modern security environment we feel that we should be able to provide releases in a more compressed timeline. The issues we ran into caused our release process to take just under four and a quarter hours from start to finish.

These issues had previously not been problematic, since the typical release process is split up over a number of days.

We’ve subsequently made a number of changes to improve our release efficiency, which should significantly reduce the time it takes us to push out a release, enhancing our ability to quickly respond to urgent security threats.

PRIVATE track security fixes are pre-announced three to seven days before their release. URGENT track fixes happen on a shorter time schedule, but we could have pre-announced the upcoming release when we began the release process, giving users at least a few hours to prepare.

While on Windows and macOS we rely on the revocation mechanisms the platform APIs provide, on Linux we don’t currently have a similar mechanism. The lack of this support was one of our major drivers to issue an expedited security release, as we did not want to leave Linux users exposed to this issue longer than was necessary.

Hence we are planning on prioritizing work to bring parity to revocation support on Linux, to help mitigate this class of issues in the future. Part of this work will involve investigating adding support for the upki project, which aims to “provide reliable, privacy-preserving and efficient certificate revocation” for Linux (see issue #82402).

Upgrading and Verifying Your Deployments

If you run Go binaries which interact with network services using TLS (such as directly via net/http or crypto/tls or via a dependency such as gRPC), ensure you are running on the latest minor releases. Binaries rebuilt with Go 1.27.3 and 1.26.10 will automatically reject certificates issued by the compromised eMudhra intermediates.

You can verify your current toolchain version using go version and you can check the version of Go a binary was built with using go version -m .

The govulncheck tool can also be used to determine if a binary is affected by this issue:

$ GOTOOLCHAIN=go1.27.3+auto go install golang.org/x/vuln/cmd/govulncheck@latest
$ govulncheck -mode=binary
Securing Go Deployments Everywhere

For us, securing Go and its users extends beyond fixing direct security vulnerabilities in the runtime and libraries we ship. In order to keep the ecosystem secure, we believe we also need to provide users with the right tools to write secure software, look towards the future of cryptographic algorithms and protocols, and proactively respond to ecosystem wide issues when we can.

We are grateful to the independent security researchers and the Mozilla security team for this rapid notification and coordination during this incident.
